t: Linear regression: closed form, gradient descent and ridge
sum: The warm-up that checks you can turn a loss into matrix code — two solvers that must agree to four decimals.
primer:
What the round is marking

An ML coding round is not a LeetCode round with NumPy. The interviewer wants to see you go from a loss function on the whiteboard to correct, vectorised code, keep the shapes straight out loud, and test what you wrote against something you can verify. Linear regression is the usual opener because the maths is small enough to derive in two minutes and still has three traps in it.

The model and the loss

  • Model: ŷ = Xw + b. X is (n, d) — n examples, d features; w is (d,); b is a scalar.
  • Loss (mean squared error): L = (1/n)·‖Xw + b − y‖².
  • Gradient: with residual r = Xw + b − y, ∂L/∂w = (2/n)·Xᵀr and ∂L/∂b = (2/n)·Σr. Say the shapes: Xᵀ is (d, n), r is (n,), so the gradient is (d,) — the same shape as w, which is the check you should do every time.
  • Closed form: set the gradient to zero and you get the normal equations XᵀX·w = Xᵀy.
  • Ridge adds α‖w‖² to the loss, which adds nα·I to XᵀX. That makes the system always solvable and shrinks the weights.

Three traps

  1. Never invert XᵀX. Solve the system (np.linalg.solve) or use least squares (np.linalg.lstsq). Inversion is slower and less accurate, and it fails outright when two columns are collinear.
  2. Do not penalise the intercept. Ridge should shrink slopes, not drag the whole prediction toward zero. Centring X and y first handles this cleanly: fit on centred data, then recover b = ȳ − x̄·w.
  3. Gradient descent needs scaled features and a bounded learning rate. If one feature is in metres and another in millimetres, the loss surface is a long thin valley and a learning rate that works for one direction diverges in the other.
body:
The problem as it is usually asked

“Implement linear regression with fit(X, y) and predict(X), without scikit-learn. Support the closed-form solution and gradient descent, and an optional L2 penalty.” Clarify before writing: is X dense and in memory? Should the intercept be fitted? How do we know gradient descent has converged?

Plan out loud

  1. Centre X and y so the intercept drops out of both solvers and is never penalised.
  2. Closed form: lstsq when there is no penalty (it survives collinear columns), solve on XᵀX + nαI when there is.
  3. Gradient descent: the same loss, the same gradient, stop when the gradient norm is tiny rather than after a fixed number of steps.
  4. Test the two solvers against each other and against the true weights of synthetic data.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

class LinearRegression:
    """Minimises (1/n)·||Xw + b - y||² + alpha·||w||²  (the intercept b is not penalised)."""

    def __init__(self, alpha=0.0, method="closed", lr=0.1, max_iter=10_000, tol=1e-8):
        self.alpha, self.method = alpha, method
        self.lr, self.max_iter, self.tol = lr, max_iter, tol

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X, y = np.asarray(X, float), np.asarray(y, float)
        n, d = X.shape
        self.x_mean, self.y_mean = X.mean(0), y.mean()
        Xc, yc = X - self.x_mean, y - self.y_mean          # centring removes the intercept
        if self.method == "closed":
            if self.alpha == 0:
                # least squares, not an inverse: stable, and fine with collinear columns
                self.w = np.linalg.lstsq(Xc, yc, rcond=None)[0]
            else:
                A = Xc.T @ Xc + n * self.alpha * np.eye(d)   # (d, d), always invertible
                self.w = np.linalg.solve(A, Xc.T @ yc)
        else:
            self.w = np.zeros(d)
            for self.n_iter in range(1, self.max_iter + 1):
                r = Xc @ self.w - yc                            # (n,) residuals
                grad = 2 * Xc.T @ r / n + 2 * self.alpha * self.w  # (d,) same shape as w
                self.w -= self.lr * grad
                if np.linalg.norm(grad) < self.tol:
                    break
        self.b = self.y_mean - self.x_mean @ self.w
        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        return np.asarray(X, float) @ self.w + self.b

Check it

Synthetic data with known weights is the fastest honest test: you know what the answer must be. Then make the two solvers agree with each other, which catches a wrong gradient immediately.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 3))
true_w, true_b = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5]), 3.0
y = X @ true_w + true_b + 0.01 * rng.normal(size=200)

closed = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
gd = LinearRegression(method="gd").fit(X, y)
assert np.allclose(closed.w, true_w, atol=0.01) and abs(closed.b - true_b) < 0.01
assert np.allclose(closed.w, gd.w, atol=1e-6) and abs(closed.b - gd.b) < 1e-6

# ridge: both solvers agree, and the weights shrink
r_closed = LinearRegression(alpha=1.0).fit(X, y)
r_gd = LinearRegression(alpha=1.0, method="gd").fit(X, y)
assert np.allclose(r_closed.w, r_gd.w, atol=1e-6)
assert np.linalg.norm(r_closed.w) < np.linalg.norm(closed.w)

# a duplicated column makes X^T X singular; lstsq still predicts correctly
X_dup = np.hstack([X, X[:, :1]])
assert np.allclose(LinearRegression().fit(X_dup, y).predict(X_dup), closed.predict(X), atol=1e-8)

Complexity

  • Closed form: O(nd²) to form XᵀX plus O(d³) to solve. Excellent up to a few thousand features.
  • Gradient descent: O(nd) per step, times the number of steps, which grows with the condition number of XᵀX. The right choice when d is large or the data streams.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Say why you are not inverting. solve factorises once; lstsq uses an SVD that tolerates rank deficiency. Forming XᵀX at all squares the condition number, which is why QR or SVD on X itself is the numerically careful route.
  • Stop on the gradient norm, not a hard-coded epoch count. It is the quantity that is exactly zero at the optimum.
  • The learning-rate bound. Gradient descent on this loss converges only if lr < 2 / λ_max, where λ_max is the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian (2/n)XᵀX + 2αI. Standardising features keeps λ_max near 2, so lr = 0.1 is safe.
  • Test against a second implementation. Two solvers that agree to six decimals is stronger evidence than any amount of re-reading.
deep:
The probabilistic reading — interviewers love this follow-up

  • MSE is Gaussian maximum likelihood. If y = Xw + ε with ε ~ N(0, σ²), the log-likelihood is −(1/2σ²)‖y − Xw‖² plus a constant, so maximising it is exactly minimising squared error.
  • Ridge is MAP with a Gaussian prior on w; the penalty strength is the ratio of noise variance to prior variance. Lasso is MAP with a Laplace prior, whose sharp peak at zero is why it produces exact zeros.

Solvers you should be able to name and place

  • QR: X = QR, then solve the triangular system Rw = Qᵀy. Never forms XᵀX, so it keeps the original condition number.
  • SVD gives the whole ridge path at once: with X = USVᵀ, w(α) = V·diag(s/(s² + nα))·Uᵀy. One decomposition, then every α is a cheap rescale — how you tune the penalty efficiently.
  • Sufficient statistics for huge n: XᵀX (d×d) and Xᵀy (d) are sums over rows, so they can be accumulated in one streaming or map-reduce pass with O(d²) memory, then solved on one machine. This is the answer to “fit it on ten billion rows”.
  • Conjugate gradient / L-BFGS when d is too large to factorise: they only need matrix–vector products and converge in far fewer steps than plain gradient descent on ill-conditioned problems.

Where plain least squares breaks

  • Outliers: squared loss lets one bad point drag the fit. Huber loss is quadratic near zero and linear in the tails.
  • Heteroscedastic noise: weighted least squares, XᵀWX·w = XᵀWy, one line different from the code above.
  • More features than rows (d > n): infinitely many exact fits. lstsq returns the minimum-norm one; ridge picks a well-defined one; that choice is a regularisation decision.
  • Multi-output: pass Y of shape (n, k). solve and lstsq handle multiple right-hand sides unchanged.
drill:
Work it out

Extend the solution to Lasso (L1 penalty), which has no closed form. Implement coordinate descent for (1/2n)·‖y − Xw‖² + α‖w‖₁ and show that it sets the weights of irrelevant features to exactly zero.

Answer

Fix every weight except w_j. The one-dimensional problem has a closed-form answer: compute the correlation ρ_j of feature j with the partial residual (the residual with j’s own contribution added back), then apply soft thresholding S(ρ, α) = sign(ρ)·max(|ρ| − α, 0). Any feature whose correlation with the residual is below α lands on exactly zero — that is where the sparsity comes from. Keep the residual up to date incrementally so each coordinate update costs O(n), not O(nd).

def soft_threshold(z, t):
    return np.sign(z) * np.maximum(np.abs(z) - t, 0.0)

def lasso_cd(X, y, alpha, n_sweeps=200):
    X = X - X.mean(0); y = y - y.mean()
    n, d = X.shape
    w = np.zeros(d)
    col_sq = (X ** 2).sum(0) / n
    r = y.copy()                                 # residual y - Xw, kept current
    for _ in range(n_sweeps):
        for j in range(d):
            r += X[:, j] * w[j]                  # add j's contribution back
            rho = X[:, j] @ r / n
            w[j] = soft_threshold(rho, alpha) / col_sq[j]
            r -= X[:, j] * w[j]
    return w

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = rng.normal(size=(300, 10))
w_true = np.zeros(10); w_true[:3] = [3.0, -2.0, 1.5]
y = X @ w_true + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=300)
w = lasso_cd(X, y, alpha=0.1)
assert np.all(w[3:] == 0.0)                     # exactly zero, not merely small
assert np.all(np.abs(w[:3] - w_true[:3]) < 0.2) # shrunk toward zero by about alpha

Two things to say out loud: the surviving weights are biased toward zero by roughly α (the price of sparsity — refit plain least squares on the selected features if you need unbiased estimates), and in practice you solve for a decreasing sequence of α values using each solution as the warm start for the next, which is how glmnet computes a whole regularisation path quickly.
qa: E
Why use np.linalg.solve or lstsq instead of inverting XᵀX?

Inversion is slower and less accurate, and it fails when columns are collinear. solve factorises the matrix once; lstsq uses an SVD that handles rank-deficient X and returns the minimum-norm solution. Forming XᵀX at all squares the condition number, so QR or SVD on X is the careful route.
M
Why should the intercept not be regularised, and how does centring handle it?

Penalising b would pull every prediction toward zero rather than shrinking slopes, and would make the fit depend on where the origin of y is. Centring X and y makes the optimal intercept zero during the solve; recover it afterwards as b = ȳ − x̄·w.
M
What learning rate makes gradient descent on MSE diverge?

Anything above 2/λ_max, where λ_max is the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian (2/n)XᵀX (+2α for ridge). Unscaled features inflate λ_max and the condition number, forcing a tiny learning rate that crawls along the flat directions — standardise first.
H
How would you fit linear regression on ten billion rows that do not fit in memory?

Accumulate the sufficient statistics XᵀX (d×d) and Xᵀy (d) in one distributed pass — they are sums over rows, so map-reduce them — then solve the small d×d system on one machine. If d itself is huge, use mini-batch SGD or conjugate gradient, which need only matrix–vector products.

sum: A numerically stable sigmoid, log-loss from logits, and the p − y gradient — the most-asked classical implementation.
primer:
From a line to a probability

Logistic regression computes a score z = Xw + b (the logit, any real number) and squashes it into a probability with the sigmoid σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)). The score is the log-odds: z = log(p / (1 − p)), so a weight is “how much one unit of this feature changes the log-odds”.

The loss: binary cross-entropy

For one example with label y ∈ {0, 1}: ℓ = −[y·log p + (1 − y)·log(1 − p)]. It is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli model — it punishes a confident wrong answer without limit, which is what you want from a probability model.

The gradient you should be able to derive on the spot

Chain the loss through the sigmoid and almost everything cancels: ∂ℓ/∂z = p − y. So for the batch, ∂L/∂w = Xᵀ(p − y)/n and ∂L/∂b = mean(p − y). It has the same form as linear regression’s gradient with p in place of ŷ — not a coincidence: both are generalised linear models with their canonical link.

Why not squared error?

MSE through a sigmoid is non-convex, and its gradient carries an extra σ′(z) factor that vanishes when the model is confidently wrong — exactly when you most need a large correction. Log-loss is convex in w, so gradient descent finds the global optimum.

The stability trap

np.exp(-z) overflows for z = −1000, and np.log(p) of a probability that rounded to 0 is −inf. A good answer computes the sigmoid without overflow and computes the loss from the logits, never from rounded probabilities.
body:
The problem

“Implement binary logistic regression trained with batch gradient descent, with optional L2 regularisation, predict_proba and predict.” Ask: are labels 0/1? Is there class imbalance? What threshold should predict use?

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    """Never overflows: exp only ever sees a non-positive argument."""
    z = np.asarray(z, float)
    out = np.empty_like(z)
    pos = z >= 0
    out[pos] = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z[pos]))
    ez = np.exp(z[~pos])
    out[~pos] = ez / (1.0 + ez)
    return out

def log_loss_from_logits(z, y):
    """mean[log(1 + e^z) - y·z] — algebraically the BCE, computed without log(0)."""
    return np.mean(np.logaddexp(0.0, z) - y * z)

class LogisticRegression:
    def __init__(self, lr=0.5, max_iter=5000, l2=0.0, tol=1e-8):
        self.lr, self.max_iter, self.l2, self.tol = lr, max_iter, l2, tol

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X, y = np.asarray(X, float), np.asarray(y, float)
        n, d = X.shape
        self.w, self.b, self.losses = np.zeros(d), 0.0, []
        for _ in range(self.max_iter):
            z = X @ self.w + self.b
            self.losses.append(log_loss_from_logits(z, y) + 0.5 * self.l2 * self.w @ self.w)
            err = sigmoid(z) - y                     # dL/dz: the whole chain rule collapses to this
            gw = X.T @ err / n + self.l2 * self.w    # (d,)
            gb = err.mean()
            self.w -= self.lr * gw
            self.b -= self.lr * gb
            if np.sqrt(gw @ gw + gb * gb) < self.tol:
                break
        return self

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        return sigmoid(np.asarray(X, float) @ self.w + self.b)

    def predict(self, X, threshold=0.5):
        return (self.predict_proba(X) >= threshold).astype(int)

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
X = rng.normal(size=(n, 2))
true_w, true_b = np.array([2.0, -3.0]), 0.5
y = (rng.random(n) < sigmoid(X @ true_w + true_b)).astype(float)   # sample labels from the true model

m = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
assert np.all(np.diff(m.losses) <= 1e-12)          # convex loss + safe step: never goes up
assert np.allclose(m.w, true_w, atol=0.4) and abs(m.b - true_b) < 0.3   # recovers the generator
assert (m.predict(X) == y).mean() > 0.8

# stability: no overflow warnings at extreme logits
with np.errstate(over="raise", invalid="raise"):
    assert np.allclose(sigmoid(np.array([-1000.0, 0.0, 1000.0])), [0.0, 0.5, 1.0])
    assert np.isfinite(log_loss_from_logits(np.array([-800.0, 800.0]), np.array([1.0, 0.0])))

# gradient check against centred finite differences
w0, b0, eps = rng.normal(size=2), 0.3, 1e-6
g = X.T @ (sigmoid(X @ w0 + b0) - y) / n
num = np.array([(log_loss_from_logits(X @ (w0 + eps * e) + b0, y)
                 - log_loss_from_logits(X @ (w0 - eps * e) + b0, y)) / (2 * eps) for e in np.eye(2)])
assert np.allclose(g, num, atol=1e-7)

Complexity

O(nd) per iteration for the two matrix–vector products. Memory O(nd) for the data plus O(d) for the model. Mini-batch SGD makes each step O(bd) for a batch of b.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Derive p − y out loud — it is the single most common follow-up, and saying “the sigmoid derivative cancels the denominator of the log” shows you understand why the model is built this way.
  • Loss from logits. log(1 + e^z) − yz is algebraically the cross-entropy and stays finite everywhere; np.logaddexp(0, z) computes log(1 + e^z) without overflow. This is what BCEWithLogitsLoss does and why it exists.
  • The threshold is not part of the model. 0.5 is only right if the costs of false positives and false negatives are equal and the probabilities are calibrated; expose it as a parameter.
  • Monotone loss is a test. For a convex loss and a safe step size, the training loss must never rise. Asserting it catches sign errors instantly.
deep:
Where the textbook model gets into trouble

  • Linearly separable data has no finite maximum-likelihood solution. The loss keeps falling as ‖w‖ → ∞: weights grow without limit and probabilities go to exactly 0 and 1. L2 regularisation (or early stopping) is what makes the optimum finite. If you see weights in the hundreds, suspect separation or a leaked feature.
  • Class imbalance. The intercept absorbs the base rate, so an unweighted model is calibrated to the training prevalence. Class weights change the loss (and break calibration); moving the threshold changes only the decision. Say which one the product needs.
  • Calibration. Unregularised logistic regression is calibrated on its training distribution by construction (the gradient condition forces the mean prediction to equal the mean label), which is one reason it remains a strong baseline and a common final layer.

Second-order methods

  • Newton / IRLS: the Hessian is XᵀSX/n with S = diag(p(1 − p)). Newton converges quadratically — typically under ten iterations — but each step costs O(nd² + d³).
  • L-BFGS approximates the curvature from recent gradients; it is scikit-learn’s default solver. For very large sparse data, SGD or coordinate methods (liblinear, SAGA) win.

Multiclass

Softmax regression replaces the sigmoid with a softmax over K logits and the gradient becomes Xᵀ(P − Y)/n with one-hot Y — the same form again. The alternative, one-vs-rest, trains K binary models and does not produce a coherent distribution. See the softmax and cross-entropy problem for the stable multiclass loss.

Follow-ups to expect

  • “Interpret a coefficient of 0.7” — each unit increase multiplies the odds by e^0.7 ≈ 2, holding the others fixed.
  • “Why is log-loss convex?” — log(1 + e^z) is convex in z, and z is linear in w.
  • “Why does feature scaling matter if the model is scale-equivariant?” — the optimum is equivalent, but the path gradient descent takes and the effect of the L2 penalty both depend on scale.
drill:
Work it out

Gradient descent above needs thousands of iterations. Implement Newton’s method (IRLS) for the same model and show it reaches the same solution in a handful of steps. What does each step cost?

Answer

Append a column of ones so the intercept is just another weight. The gradient is Xᵀ(p − y)/n; the Hessian is Xᵀ·diag(p(1 − p))·X / n. Each Newton step solves H·Δ = g and subtracts Δ. A tiny ridge term keeps H invertible if the data are separable.

def fit_newton(X, y, l2=1e-8, max_iter=50):
    Xb = np.hstack([X, np.ones((len(X), 1))])
    w = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])
    for it in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        p = sigmoid(Xb @ w)
        g = Xb.T @ (p - y) / len(y) + l2 * w
        H = (Xb * (p * (1 - p))[:, None]).T @ Xb / len(y) + l2 * np.eye(len(w))
        step = np.linalg.solve(H, g)
        w -= step
        if np.abs(step).max() < 1e-12:
            break
    return w[:-1], w[-1], it

w_n, b_n, iters = fit_newton(X, y)
assert iters <= 12                                            # quadratic convergence
assert np.allclose(w_n, m.w, atol=1e-4) and abs(b_n - m.b) < 1e-4   # same optimum as GD

Each step costs O(nd²) to build the Hessian plus O(d³) to solve it, against O(nd) for a gradient step. With d = 10 that is a bargain; with d = 10⁶ sparse features it is impossible, which is why large-scale systems use L-BFGS or SGD.
qa: E
Why is the gradient of the logistic loss simply Xᵀ(p − y)/n?

Differentiating −[y log σ(z) + (1−y) log(1−σ(z))] with respect to z gives σ(z) − y, because σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) cancels the denominators from the logs. The chain rule through z = Xw then contributes Xᵀ, and averaging over the batch gives the 1/n.
M
What happens to the weights on linearly separable data without regularisation?

They grow without bound: scaling w up always lowers the loss, so no finite maximum-likelihood solution exists. Probabilities saturate at 0 and 1. L2 regularisation or early stopping makes the optimum finite.
M
How do you compute log-loss without overflow from logits?

Use the identity BCE = log(1 + e^z) − y·z and compute log(1 + e^z) with logaddexp(0, z) (softplus). Never compute σ(z) and then take its log, because a probability that rounds to 0 or 1 gives −inf. This is what BCEWithLogitsLoss exists for.
H
Newton's method converges in a handful of iterations — why is it rarely used at scale?

Each step needs the d×d Hessian XᵀSX (O(nd²)) and a solve (O(d³)). For millions of sparse features that is infeasible in time and memory. L-BFGS approximates curvature from a few recent gradients, and SGD scales to data that does not fit in memory.

sum: Pairwise distances in one matrix multiply, top-k by partition, and a batched predict that bounds memory.
primer:
The algorithm in one sentence

To classify a point, find the k training points closest to it and take a vote. There is no training step — the “model” is the training set — which makes k-NN the simplest possible baseline and a favourite vehicle for testing whether you can vectorise.

The vocabulary

  • Distance: usually Euclidean. The squared distance is enough for ranking and avoids a square root.
  • k: small k gives a jagged, high-variance boundary; large k a smooth, high-bias one. Choose it by cross-validation.
  • Weighted voting: closer neighbours count more (weight 1/distance).
  • Feature scaling is mandatory: a feature measured in thousands swamps one measured in fractions.

What the interviewer is testing

Almost always: can you compute all query-to-training distances without a Python double loop? The trick is the expansion ‖a − b‖² = ‖a‖² − 2a·b + ‖b‖², which turns the whole distance matrix into one matrix multiply plus two broadcasts.

The obvious broadcasting version, ((A[:, None, :] − B[None, :, :])**2).sum(-1), is correct but allocates an (m, n, d) array — 100 queries × 100,000 points × 512 dimensions of float64 is 41 GB. The expansion needs only the (m, n) result.
body:
The problem

“Implement a k-NN classifier. predict must be vectorised and must work for 100,000 queries without running out of memory.” Clarify: distance metric, tie-breaking, label types (strings?), whether k can exceed the training-set size.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def pairwise_sq_dists(A, B):
    """(m, d), (n, d) -> (m, n) squared Euclidean distances via ||a||² - 2a·b + ||b||²."""
    d = (A * A).sum(1)[:, None] - 2 * A @ B.T + (B * B).sum(1)[None, :]
    return np.maximum(d, 0.0)                 # rounding can make a zero distance slightly negative

class KNNClassifier:
    def __init__(self, k=5, weighted=False):
        self.k, self.weighted = k, weighted

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X = np.asarray(X, float)
        self.classes, self.y = np.unique(y, return_inverse=True)   # any label type -> 0..C-1
        return self

    def predict(self, Xq, batch=1024):
        Xq = np.asarray(Xq, float)
        k = min(self.k, len(self.X))
        out = []
        for s in range(0, len(Xq), batch):                 # memory is batch × n, not m × n
            d = pairwise_sq_dists(Xq[s:s + batch], self.X)
            idx = np.argpartition(d, k - 1, axis=1)[:, :k]  # k smallest per row in O(n), unordered
            rows = np.arange(len(d))[:, None]
            w = 1.0 / (np.sqrt(d[rows, idx]) + 1e-12) if self.weighted else np.ones(idx.shape)
            votes = np.zeros((len(d), len(self.classes)))
            np.add.at(votes, (np.broadcast_to(rows, idx.shape), self.y[idx]), w)
            out.append(self.classes[votes.argmax(1)])
        return np.concatenate(out)

Check it

Test the vectorised distance against a loop, then the whole classifier against a deliberately naive sort-based version.

A, B = rng.normal(size=(7, 4)), rng.normal(size=(5, 4))
loop = np.array([[((a - b) ** 2).sum() for b in B] for a in A])
assert np.allclose(pairwise_sq_dists(A, B), loop)

X = np.vstack([rng.normal(0, 1, (100, 2)), rng.normal(3, 1, (100, 2))])
y = np.array([0] * 100 + [1] * 100)
Xq = rng.normal(1.5, 2, (50, 2))

def brute(q, k=7):
    nn = np.argsort(((X - q) ** 2).sum(1))[:k]
    return np.bincount(y[nn], minlength=2).argmax()

knn = KNNClassifier(k=7).fit(X, y)
assert (knn.predict(Xq, batch=16) == np.array([brute(q) for q in Xq])).all()   # batching changes nothing

labels = np.where(y == 1, "cat", "dog")
assert (KNNClassifier(k=1).fit(X, labels).predict(X) == labels).all()

Complexity

  • Time: O(m·n·d) for the distance matrix (a BLAS matmul, so fast in practice) plus O(m·n) for the partition. A full argsort would be O(m·n log n).
  • Memory: O(batch·n) per chunk. Without batching, 100k queries against 1M points is 800 GB of float64.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Clamp at zero after the expansion: cancellation can produce −1e−15, and sqrt of that is NaN.
  • argpartition, not argsort: you need the k smallest, not a full ordering. Say the complexity difference.
  • np.add.at for the vote: plain fancy-index assignment votes[r, c] += w silently drops repeated indices; add.at accumulates them.
  • Ties: argmax picks the lowest class index. Mention alternatives — odd k for binary problems, weighted votes, or falling back to the single nearest neighbour.
deep:
Why k-NN degrades, and what replaces brute force

  • The curse of dimensionality. In high dimensions the nearest and farthest neighbours are almost equally far, so “nearest” carries little information unless the data lie on a low-dimensional manifold (which embeddings usually do — that is why k-NN over learned embeddings works well).
  • Space-partitioning trees (KD-tree, ball tree) give roughly O(log n) queries in low dimensions (d ≲ 20) and degrade to brute force above that.
  • Approximate nearest neighbour indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude of speed: HNSW (graph), IVF (cluster then search a few lists), product quantisation (compress vectors to bytes). This is the vector-database layer under every RAG system.
  • Exact search on a GPU is often good enough up to a few million vectors — the distance matrix is a matmul, and GPUs are matmul machines.

Metric choices

  • Cosine similarity for embeddings: normalise the vectors once and the dot product is the cosine, and squared Euclidean distance becomes 2 − 2·cos, so the rankings agree.
  • Mahalanobis distance accounts for feature correlations; metric-learning methods learn the matrix.

Practical points

  • k-NN regression averages neighbour targets instead of voting.
  • Leave-one-out cross-validation is almost free for k-NN: compute the training-to-training distance matrix once, mask the diagonal and evaluate every k from one sort.
  • Prediction cost grows with the training set, so k-NN is cheap to train and expensive to serve — the opposite of a parametric model.
drill:
Work it out

Choose k by leave-one-out cross-validation without refitting anything. Evaluate every k in [1, 3, 5, …, 25] using a single distance computation and a single sort.

Answer

Compute the training-to-training distance matrix, set the diagonal to infinity so a point cannot vote for itself, and sort each row once. The first k columns of that order are the neighbours for every k at once.

def loo_accuracy(X, y, ks):
    d = pairwise_sq_dists(X, X)
    np.fill_diagonal(d, np.inf)                   # leave one out: never your own neighbour
    order = np.argsort(d, axis=1)                  # one sort serves every k
    C = y.max() + 1
    acc = {}
    for k in ks:
        nbr = y[order[:, :k]]                      # (n, k) neighbour labels
        votes = np.stack([(nbr == c).sum(1) for c in range(C)], axis=1)
        acc[k] = float((votes.argmax(1) == y).mean())
    return acc

Xn = np.vstack([rng.normal(0, 1.5, (150, 2)), rng.normal(2, 1.5, (150, 2))])   # overlapping classes
yn = np.array([0] * 150 + [1] * 150)
acc = loo_accuracy(Xn, yn, range(1, 26, 2))
assert max(acc, key=acc.get) > 1                  # with overlapping classes, k = 1 overfits

Accuracy usually rises from k = 1, peaks, then falls as the neighbourhood starts including the other class — the bias–variance trade-off in one curve. The cost is one O(n²d) distance matrix and one O(n² log n) sort, instead of a model fit per fold per k.

Why expand ‖a − b‖² instead of broadcasting A[:, None] − B[None]?

The broadcast allocates an (m, n, d) intermediate — often tens of gigabytes. The expansion ‖a‖² − 2a·b + ‖b‖² needs only the (m, n) result and turns the heavy part into one BLAS matrix multiply. Clamp the result at zero because cancellation can make it slightly negative.
M
Why argpartition rather than argsort for the k nearest?

argpartition finds the k smallest in O(n) per row without ordering them; argsort is O(n log n) and orders everything. You only need the set of k neighbours for a vote, so the full sort is wasted work.

Why must features be standardised for k-NN?

Distance sums squared differences across features, so a feature with a large numeric range dominates the metric regardless of how informative it is. Standardising (or learning a metric) puts the features on a comparable scale.

How would you serve k-NN over 100 million embeddings at 10 ms per query?

Brute force is ~100M×d multiply-adds per query — too slow on CPU. Use an approximate index: HNSW for high recall and low latency in memory, or IVF with product quantisation to compress vectors to tens of bytes so the index fits in RAM. Tune recall@k against latency, and re-rank the ANN candidates with exact distances.

sum: Lloyd's two alternating steps, a seeding that spreads the centres, empty clusters and restarts.
primer:
The goal

Split n points into k groups so that each point is close to its group’s centre. Formally, minimise the inertia — the sum of squared distances from each point to its assigned centre.

Lloyd’s algorithm: two steps, repeated

  1. Assign: give each point to its nearest centre.
  2. Update: move each centre to the mean of its points.

Each step can only lower the inertia (the nearest centre is the best assignment for fixed centres; the mean is the best centre for a fixed assignment), and there are finitely many assignments, so the algorithm always stops. It stops at a local minimum, though, which depends on where the centres started.

Why the starting centres matter

Random initial centres often land two in one true cluster and none in another, and Lloyd cannot fix that. k-means++ picks the first centre at random, then each next centre with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest centre chosen so far. Far-away regions get seeded, and the expected result is provably within O(log k) of optimal before Lloyd even starts.

Two practical details

  • Empty clusters: a centre can lose all its points. Re-seed it at the point that is currently worst served.
  • Restarts: run several times from different seeds and keep the lowest inertia.
body:
The problem

“Implement k-means. Return the centres, the labels and the inertia.” Clarify: how to initialise, when to stop, what to do with an empty cluster, and whether restarts are expected.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def sq_dists(X, C):
    return np.maximum((X * X).sum(1)[:, None] - 2 * X @ C.T + (C * C).sum(1)[None, :], 0.0)

def kmeans_pp(X, k, rng):
    centres = [X[rng.integers(len(X))]]
    d2 = ((X - centres[0]) ** 2).sum(1)              # squared distance to the nearest centre so far
    for _ in range(1, k):
        c = X[rng.choice(len(X), p=d2 / d2.sum())]   # far points are more likely to be picked
        centres.append(c)
        d2 = np.minimum(d2, ((X - c) ** 2).sum(1))
    return np.array(centres)

def lloyd(X, C, max_iter=300, tol=1e-9):
    history = []
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        d = sq_dists(X, C)
        labels = d.argmin(1)                                   # assign step
        history.append(d[np.arange(len(X)), labels].sum())
        new_C = C.copy()
        for j in range(len(C)):                                # update step
            members = labels == j
            if members.any():
                new_C[j] = X[members].mean(0)
            else:                                              # empty: re-seed at the worst-served point
                new_C[j] = X[d[np.arange(len(X)), labels].argmax()]
        converged = np.abs(new_C - C).max() < tol
        C = new_C
        if converged:
            break
    d = sq_dists(X, C)
    labels = d.argmin(1)
    return C, labels, d[np.arange(len(X)), labels].sum(), history

def kmeans(X, k, n_init=5, seed=0):
    X = np.asarray(X, float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    runs = [lloyd(X, kmeans_pp(X, k, rng)) for _ in range(n_init)]
    C, labels, inertia, _ = min(runs, key=lambda r: r[2])    # keep the best restart
    return C, labels, inertia

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
true_C = np.array([[0, 0], [8, 0], [4, 7]], float)
X = np.vstack([c + rng.normal(0, 0.7, (200, 2)) for c in true_C])
truth = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], 200)

C, labels, inertia = kmeans(X, 3)
# centres recovered up to permutation
match = sq_dists(true_C, C).argmin(1)
assert sorted(match) == [0, 1, 2] and np.allclose(C[match], true_C, atol=0.2)
# every true cluster maps to exactly one found cluster
assert all(len(set(labels[truth == t])) == 1 for t in range(3))

# Lloyd never increases the inertia, even from a deliberately bad start
_, _, _, hist = lloyd(X, X[:3].copy())
assert np.all(np.diff(hist) <= 1e-9)

# an empty cluster is re-seeded rather than left as NaN
C_bad = np.array([[0, 0], [8, 0], [4, 7], [100, 100]], float)
C4, _, _, _ = lloyd(X, C_bad)
assert np.isfinite(C4).all()

Complexity

O(n·k·d) per iteration for the distances, times the number of iterations (usually tens), times the restarts. k-means++ seeding is O(n·k·d) once.

Details that separate a good answer

  • State the convergence argument: both steps are non-increasing in inertia and the number of partitions is finite. Then say “but only to a local minimum”, which motivates k-means++ and restarts.
  • Handle the empty cluster explicitly — the mean of zero points is NaN, and it silently poisons every later iteration.
  • Vectorise the assignment with the distance expansion; the update loop over k is fine because k is small.
  • Test on blobs with known centres, comparing up to a permutation — cluster ids are arbitrary.
deep:
What k-means assumes, and what to use when it is wrong

  • It minimises squared Euclidean distance, so it prefers convex, roughly spherical clusters of similar size. It splits elongated clusters and merges small ones into big neighbours.
  • Gaussian mixture models generalise it with per-cluster covariance and soft assignments (k-means is the limit of a GMM with shared, shrinking isotropic variance). DBSCAN / HDBSCAN find arbitrary shapes and label noise. Spectral clustering handles non-convex structure via a graph.
  • Choosing k: the elbow of inertia versus k is ambiguous in practice; silhouette score, gap statistic, or a downstream metric are better. Often k is a product decision (how many segments can marketing act on?).

At scale

  • Mini-batch k-means updates centres from small random batches with per-centre learning rates — orders of magnitude faster, slightly worse inertia.
  • k-means|| (scalable k-means++) oversamples candidate centres in a few parallel rounds instead of k sequential ones — the default in Spark MLlib.
  • Distributed Lloyd: broadcast the centres, each worker assigns its shard and emits per-cluster sums and counts, a reduce computes the new means. The communication is only O(k·d) per iteration.
  • Large k (the IVF index in a vector database trains k-means with thousands of centres): the assignment step becomes a nearest-neighbour search itself, so it is accelerated with the same ANN tricks.

Connections worth mentioning

  • k-means on embeddings is how product quantisation codebooks and IVF partitions are built.
  • It is also the E and M steps of EM with hard assignments — a good way to show you see the family resemblance.
drill:
Work it out

Implement the silhouette score and use it to choose k between 2 and 6 on the three-blob data above. For point i, a(i) is the mean distance to the other points in its cluster and b(i) the mean distance to the points of the nearest other cluster; s(i) = (b − a) / max(a, b).

Answer 
def silhouette(X, labels):
    D = np.sqrt(sq_dists(X, X))
    ks = np.unique(labels)
    s = np.zeros(len(X))
    for i in range(len(X)):
        own = labels == labels[i]
        if own.sum() == 1:
            continue                                    # singleton: silhouette defined as 0
        a = D[i, own].sum() / (own.sum() - 1)           # exclude the point itself (distance 0)
        b = min(D[i, labels == c].mean() for c in ks if c != labels[i])
        s[i] = (b - a) / max(a, b)
    return s.mean()

scores = {k: silhouette(X, kmeans(X, k)[1]) for k in range(2, 7)}
assert max(scores, key=scores.get) == 3

The silhouette rewards tight, well-separated clusters and is bounded in [−1, 1], so unlike inertia it does not keep improving as k grows. Its cost is O(n²) — sample a few thousand points on large data. The elbow on inertia would be visible here too, but on real data it is rarely this clear.
qa: E
Why use k-means++ rather than random initial centres?

Random centres can land several in one true cluster and none in another, and Lloyd's algorithm cannot move a centre across that gap. k-means++ samples each new centre with probability proportional to squared distance from the existing ones, spreading them out; it is O(log k)-competitive in expectation and converges faster.
M
Does Lloyd's algorithm always converge, and to what?

Yes: the assign step and the update step each never increase inertia, and there are finitely many partitions, so it terminates. But only at a local minimum that depends on the initialisation — hence restarts, keeping the lowest inertia.
M
What cluster shapes does k-means handle badly?

Non-convex shapes (rings, moons), elongated or anisotropic clusters, and clusters of very different sizes or densities, because it minimises squared Euclidean distance to a single centre. Use a GMM for anisotropy, DBSCAN/HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise, spectral clustering for non-convex structure.
H
How do you run k-means on a billion points?

Seed with k-means|| (a few parallel oversampling rounds) and run distributed Lloyd: broadcast centres, each worker assigns its shard and emits per-cluster sums and counts, reduce into new means — O(k·d) communication per iteration. Or use mini-batch k-means on samples. With very large k, accelerate assignment with an ANN index.

sum: Gini impurity, the best-split scan with cumulative counts, recursion with stopping rules, and prediction by walking the tree.
primer:
How a tree predicts

A decision tree is a flowchart of yes/no questions of the form “is feature j ≤ threshold t?”. Each leaf holds the class proportions of the training points that ended there. To predict, walk from the root, answering each question, until you reach a leaf.

How it is built: greedy splitting

At each node, try every feature and every threshold between consecutive distinct values, and keep the split that makes the two children purest. Recurse on each child. Stop when the node is pure, too small, or too deep.

Impurity

  • Gini: 1 − Σ p_c². Zero for a pure node, 0.5 for a 50/50 binary node. The chance of mislabelling a random point if you labelled it randomly by the node’s class distribution.
  • Entropy: −Σ p_c log p_c. Choosing the split that most reduces it is “information gain”.
  • The two almost always choose the same split; Gini avoids a logarithm.
  • A split’s quality is the size-weighted impurity of its children: (n_L·G_L + n_R·G_R) / n.

The efficient scan

Evaluating each threshold from scratch is O(n) per threshold, O(n²) per feature. Instead, sort the feature once and sweep left to right: moving one point from the right child to the left changes the class counts by one. With cumulative sums the whole sweep is vectorised, and the cost per feature is dominated by the O(n log n) sort.
body:
The problem

“Implement a decision tree classifier with max_depth and min_samples_split, using Gini impurity. Include predict_proba.” Clarify: numeric features only? Multiclass? How are ties between equal feature values handled?

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("feature", "threshold", "left", "right", "proba")
    def __init__(self, proba=None, feature=None, threshold=None, left=None, right=None):
        self.proba, self.feature, self.threshold, self.left, self.right = proba, feature, threshold, left, right

def gini_of_counts(counts):
    n = counts.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    return 1.0 - ((counts / n) ** 2).sum(-1)

class DecisionTree:
    def __init__(self, max_depth=5, min_samples_split=2):
        self.max_depth, self.min_samples_split = max_depth, min_samples_split

    def fit(self, X, y):
        X = np.asarray(X, float)
        self.classes, y = np.unique(y, return_inverse=True)
        self.K = len(self.classes)
        self.root = self._grow(X, y, depth=0)
        return self

    def best_split(self, X, y):
        n = len(y)
        parent = np.bincount(y, minlength=self.K)
        best_imp, best = gini_of_counts(parent), (None, None)   # a split must beat the parent
        for f in range(X.shape[1]):
            order = np.argsort(X[:, f], kind="stable")
            xs, ys = X[order, f], y[order]
            left = np.cumsum(np.eye(self.K)[ys], axis=0)[:-1]    # counts left of each cut, (n-1, K)
            right = parent - left
            n_left = np.arange(1, n)
            imp = (n_left * gini_of_counts(left) + (n - n_left) * gini_of_counts(right)) / n
            imp[xs[1:] == xs[:-1]] = np.inf                        # cannot cut between equal values
            i = int(imp.argmin())
            if imp[i] < best_imp - 1e-12:
                best_imp, best = imp[i], (f, (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2)
        return best

    def _grow(self, X, y, depth):
        counts = np.bincount(y, minlength=self.K)
        leaf = Node(proba=counts / counts.sum())
        if depth == self.max_depth or len(y) < self.min_samples_split or counts.max() == len(y):
            return leaf
        f, t = self.best_split(X, y)
        if f is None:                                              # no split reduces impurity
            return leaf
        m = X[:, f] <= t
        return Node(feature=f, threshold=t,
                    left=self._grow(X[m], y[m], depth + 1),
                    right=self._grow(X[~m], y[~m], depth + 1))

    def _leaf(self, x):
        node = self.root
        while node.proba is None:
            node = node.left if x[node.feature] <= node.threshold else node.right
        return node

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        return np.array([self._leaf(x).proba for x in np.asarray(X, float)])

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.classes[self.predict_proba(X).argmax(1)]

Check it

Test the vectorised split search against a brute-force search that recomputes Gini for every candidate threshold, then test the tree’s behaviour.

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def brute_best(X, y, K):
    def g(lab): return 1 - ((np.bincount(lab, minlength=K) / len(lab)) ** 2).sum()
    best = (g(y), None, None)
    for f in range(X.shape[1]):
        vals = np.unique(X[:, f])
        for t in (vals[:-1] + vals[1:]) / 2:
            m = X[:, f] <= t
            imp = (m.sum() * g(y[m]) + (~m).sum() * g(y[~m])) / len(y)
            if imp < best[0] - 1e-12:
                best = (imp, f, t)
    return best[1], best[2]

for trial in range(20):
    Xs = rng.integers(0, 6, size=(40, 3)).astype(float)       # many ties on purpose
    ys = rng.integers(0, 3, size=40)
    tree = DecisionTree().fit(Xs, ys)
    assert tree.best_split(Xs, ys) == brute_best(Xs, ys, 3)

# an axis-aligned rectangle needs exactly two splits
X = rng.random((500, 2))
y = ((X[:, 0] > 0.3) & (X[:, 1] < 0.6)).astype(int)
assert (DecisionTree(max_depth=2).fit(X, y).predict(X) == y).all()

# a fully grown tree memorises any data without duplicate points
yr = rng.integers(0, 2, 500)
assert (DecisionTree(max_depth=100).fit(X, yr).predict(X) == yr).all()

# greedy myopia: exact XOR — no single split lowers impurity, so the root stays a leaf
Xx = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], float); yx = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0])
assert DecisionTree(max_depth=5).fit(Xx, yx).root.proba is not None

Complexity

  • Training: each level of the tree sorts every feature over all points once: O(d·n log n) per level, O(d·n log n·depth) overall.
  • Prediction: O(depth) per point.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Cannot cut between equal values. Masking those positions is the bug most hand-written trees have — the brute-force test uses integer features precisely to exercise it.
  • A split must beat the parent. Otherwise the tree splits on noise with zero gain and the XOR example shows the consequence of a purely greedy criterion.
  • Thresholds at midpoints between consecutive distinct values, so unseen values between them are routed sensibly.
  • Stopping rules are the regularisation. An unrestricted tree memorises the training set, as the test shows.
deep:
How production libraries differ from this code

  • Histogram splitting (LightGBM, XGBoost hist, scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting): bucket each feature into ≤ 256 bins once, then a node's split search is O(n) to fill histograms plus O(bins) to scan them. No per-node sorting.
  • The subtraction trick: a child's histogram is the parent's minus its sibling's, so only the smaller child needs to be built.
  • Missing values: XGBoost learns a default direction per split by trying the missing rows on each side and keeping the better one.
  • Categorical features: for binary classification the optimal partition of categories is found by sorting categories by their positive rate and scanning like a numeric feature (Fisher, 1958); LightGBM does this with gradient statistics.

Controlling variance

  • Single trees are high-variance: a small change in data can change the root split and the whole tree. Bagging and random forests (random feature subsets per split) average that variance away; boosting fits shallow trees sequentially to reduce bias.
  • Cost-complexity pruning grows a full tree and prunes back with a penalty α per leaf, choosing α by cross-validation — more principled than a depth limit.

Feature importance and its trap

Impurity-based importance (total impurity decrease per feature) is biased toward high-cardinality features, which offer more thresholds to overfit on. Permutation importance on held-out data, or SHAP values, are the defensible alternatives.
drill:
Work it out

Turn the classifier into a regression tree: the split criterion becomes the reduction in squared error, and a leaf predicts the mean. Keep the split search vectorised — what replaces the cumulative class counts?

Answer

The sum of squared errors of a group is Σy² − (Σy)²/n, so cumulative sums of y and y² along the sorted order give the SSE of every left and right child in one pass.

def best_regression_split(X, y, min_leaf=1):
    n, best = len(y), (((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum(), None, None)
    for f in range(X.shape[1]):
        o = np.argsort(X[:, f], kind="stable")
        xs, ys = X[o, f], y[o]
        s, s2 = np.cumsum(ys), np.cumsum(ys * ys)
        nl = np.arange(1, n); nr = n - nl
        sse = (s2[:-1] - s[:-1] ** 2 / nl) + ((s2[-1] - s2[:-1]) - (s[-1] - s[:-1]) ** 2 / nr)
        sse[(xs[1:] == xs[:-1]) | (nl < min_leaf) | (nr < min_leaf)] = np.inf
        i = int(sse.argmin())
        if sse[i] < best[0] - 1e-9:
            best = (sse[i], f, (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2)
    return best[1], best[2]

Xr = rng.random((300, 2))
yr = np.where(Xr[:, 1] > 0.7, 5.0, 1.0) + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=300)
f, t = best_regression_split(Xr, yr)
assert f == 1 and abs(t - 0.7) < 0.05          # finds the step in feature 1

The rest of the tree is unchanged: leaves store the mean of their targets, and the prediction walk is identical. This vectorised SSE scan is exactly the inner loop of gradient boosting, where the targets are residuals — see the next problem.
qa: E
Gini or entropy — does the choice matter?

Rarely. Both are concave impurity measures that are zero for pure nodes and maximal for uniform ones, and they choose the same split in the vast majority of cases. Gini is slightly cheaper because it avoids a logarithm; entropy corresponds to information gain.
M
Why can a greedy tree not learn exact XOR with one split, even at depth 2?

On balanced XOR every single split leaves both children 50/50, so no first split reduces impurity and a gain-requiring tree stops at the root. Greedy splitting is myopic — it cannot see that two splits together would be perfect. Noise in real data breaks the tie; ensembles and lookahead are the principled fixes.
M
What does finding the best split cost, and how do libraries make it faster?

Naively O(d·n log n) per node for the sorts. Histogram methods bin each feature once into ≤256 buckets, so a node costs O(n·d) to fill histograms plus O(bins·d) to scan them, and a child's histogram can be derived by subtracting its sibling's from the parent's.
H
How do XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values and categorical features?

Missing values: at each split, try sending all missing rows left and then right, and keep the better direction as the learned default. Categoricals: sort the categories by a target statistic (gradient over hessian) and scan them as if ordered, which finds the optimal binary partition without trying 2^k subsets; or one-hot encode for low cardinality.

sum: Functional gradient descent: fit a small tree to the residuals, take a shrunken step, repeat.
primer:
The idea

Start with a constant prediction — the mean. Look at what is still wrong (the residuals), fit a small tree to predict those residuals, and add a fraction of that tree’s prediction to your model. Repeat a few hundred times. Each tree corrects the mistakes of the ensemble so far.

Why “gradient” boosting

For squared loss ½(y − F)², the negative gradient with respect to the prediction F is exactly the residual y − F. So “fit a tree to the residuals” is “fit a tree to the negative gradient” — gradient descent, but taking steps in the space of functions rather than parameters. For other losses (log-loss, Huber, quantile) you fit the tree to that loss’s negative gradient, the pseudo-residual.

The knobs

  • Learning rate (shrinkage) — the fraction of each tree you add, typically 0.05–0.1. Smaller rates need more trees but generalise better.
  • Number of trees — chosen by early stopping on validation loss.
  • Tree depth — 3 to 8. Depth controls how many features can interact inside one tree.
  • Subsampling — fitting each tree on a random fraction of rows (stochastic gradient boosting) adds regularisation and speed.

Contrast with random forests

A random forest grows deep, independent trees in parallel and averages them — it reduces variance. Boosting grows shallow trees sequentially, each depending on the previous — it reduces bias. That is why boosting usually wins on accuracy and why it overfits if you do not stop it.
body:
The problem

“Implement gradient boosting for regression with squared loss. Include learning rate, number of trees, tree depth and row subsampling.” A regression tree is part of the answer, so write a compact one (the vectorised SSE scan from the decision-tree problem).

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def fit_tree(X, g, depth, min_leaf=5):
    """Least-squares regression tree on targets g; nodes are tuples."""
    n = len(g)
    if depth == 0 or n < 2 * min_leaf:
        return ("leaf", g.mean())
    best = (np.inf, None, None)
    for f in range(X.shape[1]):
        o = np.argsort(X[:, f], kind="stable")
        xs, gs = X[o, f], g[o]
        s, s2 = np.cumsum(gs), np.cumsum(gs * gs)
        nl = np.arange(1, n); nr = n - nl
        sse = (s2[:-1] - s[:-1] ** 2 / nl) + ((s2[-1] - s2[:-1]) - (s[-1] - s[:-1]) ** 2 / nr)
        sse[(xs[1:] == xs[:-1]) | (nl < min_leaf) | (nr < min_leaf)] = np.inf
        i = int(sse.argmin())
        if sse[i] < best[0]:
            best = (sse[i], f, (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2)
    if best[1] is None:
        return ("leaf", g.mean())
    _, f, t = best
    m = X[:, f] <= t
    return ("split", f, t, fit_tree(X[m], g[m], depth - 1, min_leaf),
                           fit_tree(X[~m], g[~m], depth - 1, min_leaf))

def predict_tree(node, X):
    if node[0] == "leaf":
        return np.full(len(X), node[1])
    _, f, t, left, right = node
    m = X[:, f] <= t
    out = np.empty(len(X))
    out[m], out[~m] = predict_tree(left, X[m]), predict_tree(right, X[~m])
    return out

class GradientBoostingRegressor:
    def __init__(self, n_trees=200, lr=0.1, depth=3, subsample=1.0, seed=0):
        self.n_trees, self.lr, self.depth, self.subsample, self.seed = n_trees, lr, depth, subsample, seed

    def fit(self, X, y, X_val=None, y_val=None):
        X, y = np.asarray(X, float), np.asarray(y, float)
        rng = np.random.default_rng(self.seed)
        self.f0 = y.mean()                               # best constant under squared loss
        F = np.full(len(y), self.f0)
        self.trees, self.train_loss, self.val_loss = [], [], []
        F_val = None if X_val is None else np.full(len(X_val), self.f0)
        for _ in range(self.n_trees):
            residual = y - F                             # negative gradient of ½(y - F)²
            rows = rng.random(len(y)) < self.subsample if self.subsample < 1 else np.ones(len(y), bool)
            tree = fit_tree(X[rows], residual[rows], self.depth)
            F += self.lr * predict_tree(tree, X)         # shrunken step in function space
            self.trees.append(tree)
            self.train_loss.append(np.mean((y - F) ** 2))
            if F_val is not None:
                F_val += self.lr * predict_tree(tree, X_val)
                self.val_loss.append(np.mean((y_val - F_val) ** 2))
        return self

    def predict(self, X, n_trees=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, float)
        return self.f0 + self.lr * sum(predict_tree(t, X) for t in self.trees[:n_trees])

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def make(n):
    X = rng.uniform(-3, 3, (n, 2))
    return X, np.sin(X[:, 0]) + 0.5 * X[:, 1] ** 2 + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=n)
X, y = make(600)
Xv, yv = make(400)

gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(n_trees=200, lr=0.1, depth=3).fit(X, y, Xv, yv)
# full-batch squared loss with leaf means and lr <= 1: training loss never increases
assert np.all(np.diff(gb.train_loss) <= 1e-12)
# the ensemble beats a single tree of the same depth, and the constant baseline, on held-out data
single = np.mean((yv - predict_tree(fit_tree(X, y, 3), Xv)) ** 2)
assert gb.val_loss[-1] < 0.5 * single and gb.val_loss[-1] < 0.1 * np.var(yv)
# predict() reproduces the incrementally tracked validation predictions
assert np.isclose(np.mean((yv - gb.predict(Xv)) ** 2), gb.val_loss[-1])
# early stopping: the best validation round is where you would truncate
best_round = int(np.argmin(gb.val_loss)) + 1
assert np.mean((yv - gb.predict(Xv, best_round)) ** 2) <= gb.val_loss[-1] + 1e-12

Complexity

Training is n_trees × O(d·n log n·depth) with the sorting tree above (histogram trees remove the log). Prediction is O(n_trees·depth) per row — cheap, which is why GBDTs dominate low-latency tabular serving.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Initialise with the loss-optimal constant: the mean for squared loss, the log-odds of the base rate for log-loss, the median for absolute loss.
  • Every tree is evaluated on all rows, even when it was fitted on a subsample; otherwise the running prediction F is wrong for the rows left out.
  • Track validation loss per round — early stopping is how the number of trees is chosen in practice, and it is almost free when you keep the running validation prediction.
  • The monotone-loss assertion holds because a least-squares tree's fitted values are a projection of the residual: adding any fraction up to 1 of it cannot increase the squared error.
deep:
XGBoost's second-order view

  • Expand the loss to second order around the current prediction: each row contributes a gradient g_i and a hessian h_i. For a leaf containing rows I, the optimal weight is w* = −G/(H + λ) with G = Σg_i, H = Σh_i.
  • The gain of a split is ½[G_L²/(H_L+λ) + G_R²/(H_R+λ) − G²/(H+λ)] − γ. λ shrinks leaf weights; γ is a minimum gain per extra leaf — both are regularisation built into the split search.
  • Any twice-differentiable loss plugs in by supplying g and h: log-loss gives g = p − y, h = p(1 − p).

Why GBDTs still beat deep networks on tabular data

Tabular features are heterogeneous (units, scales, categories), the target is often irregular in feature space, and many columns are uninformative. Trees are invariant to monotone transforms, ignore useless features cheaply and represent sharp thresholds naturally; networks are biased toward smooth functions. Benchmarks such as Grinsztajn et al. (2022) find tuned GBDTs ahead on medium-sized tabular data.

Production details

  • Leaf-wise vs depth-wise growth: LightGBM grows the leaf with the largest gain anywhere in the tree — more accurate per leaf, more prone to overfit on small data (limit num_leaves).
  • Monotone constraints (price must not increase predicted churn…) are supported by all major libraries and are often a regulatory requirement.
  • Serving: hundreds of trees compile to branchy code; libraries such as Treelite or ONNX runtimes batch and vectorise tree evaluation.
  • Explanations: TreeSHAP computes exact Shapley values for tree ensembles in polynomial time — the standard way to explain individual GBDT predictions.
drill:
Work it out

Switch to binary classification with log-loss. What is the initial prediction, what are the pseudo-residuals, and what should a leaf's value be? Implement it by reusing fit_tree for the tree structure.

Answer

Work in log-odds. Initialise F₀ = log(p̄ / (1 − p̄)). The pseudo-residual is y − p with p = σ(F). The squared-error tree fitted to it gives the structure, but its leaf means are the wrong step size; the Newton step for a leaf is Σ(y − p) / Σp(1 − p) over the rows in that leaf. So re-weight the leaves after fitting.

def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def leaf_ids(node, X, path=0):
    if node[0] == "leaf":
        return np.full(len(X), path)
    _, f, t, l, r = node
    m = X[:, f] <= t
    out = np.empty(len(X), int)
    out[m], out[~m] = leaf_ids(l, X[m], 2 * path + 1), leaf_ids(r, X[~m], 2 * path + 2)
    return out

def boost_logloss(X, y, n_trees=100, lr=0.1, depth=3):
    p0 = y.mean()
    F = np.full(len(y), np.log(p0 / (1 - p0)))
    losses = []
    for _ in range(n_trees):
        p = sigmoid(F)
        tree = fit_tree(X, y - p, depth)                  # structure from the pseudo-residuals
        ids = leaf_ids(tree, X)
        step = np.zeros(len(y))
        for leaf in np.unique(ids):
            m = ids == leaf                              # Newton step per leaf
            step[m] = (y[m] - p[m]).sum() / ((p[m] * (1 - p[m])).sum() + 1e-12)
        F += lr * step
        losses.append(np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, F) - y * F))
    return F, losses

Xc = rng.uniform(-3, 3, (500, 2))
yc = (Xc[:, 0] ** 2 + Xc[:, 1] ** 2 < 4).astype(float)     # a circle: not linearly separable
F, losses = boost_logloss(Xc, yc)
assert losses[-1] < 0.3 * losses[0] and ((F > 0) == yc).mean() > 0.95

This is the mechanism XGBoost generalises: gradient for the structure, gradient over hessian for the leaf weights, with λ added to the denominator as regularisation.

sum: Multinomial NB with Laplace smoothing, computed in log space so a long document cannot underflow.
primer:
Bayes’ rule for classification

Pick the class with the highest posterior: P(c | doc) ∝ P(c)·P(doc | c). The prior P(c) is the class frequency. The hard part is P(doc | c).

The naive assumption

Assume the words are conditionally independent given the class. Then P(doc | c) = Π P(w | c) over the words in the document, and each P(w | c) is just “how often does word w appear in class c documents, out of all words in class c”. Training is counting.

Two problems and their fixes

  • Zero counts. A word never seen in spam gives P(w | spam) = 0, and the product is 0 no matter what else the document says. Laplace (add-α) smoothing adds α to every count: P(w | c) = (count + α) / (total + α·V) for vocabulary size V.
  • Underflow. Multiplying hundreds of probabilities around 10⁻⁴ gives numbers far below the smallest float, which round to exactly 0. Work in log space: sum log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities.

Why it is still worth knowing

It trains in one pass, handles huge vocabularies, needs little data, and is a strong baseline for short-text classification — and it is a clean test of whether you can do probability arithmetic safely in code.
body:
The problem

“Implement a multinomial Naive Bayes text classifier with Laplace smoothing. fit(docs, labels), predict, predict_log_proba.” Clarify: tokenisation (whitespace is fine), how to treat words not seen in training, multiclass support.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

class MultinomialNB:
    def __init__(self, alpha=1.0):
        self.alpha = alpha

    def fit(self, docs, labels):
        self.vocab = {w: i for i, w in enumerate(sorted({w for d in docs for w in d.split()}))}
        self.classes = sorted(set(labels))
        K, V = len(self.classes), len(self.vocab)
        counts, prior = np.zeros((K, V)), np.zeros(K)
        for doc, label in zip(docs, labels):
            k = self.classes.index(label)
            prior[k] += 1
            for w, c in Counter(doc.split()).items():
                counts[k, self.vocab[w]] += c
        self.log_prior = np.log(prior / prior.sum())
        smoothed = counts + self.alpha                   # no word ever has probability 0
        self.log_lik = np.log(smoothed / smoothed.sum(1, keepdims=True))   # (K, V)
        return self

    def _counts(self, docs):
        X = np.zeros((len(docs), len(self.vocab)))
        for r, doc in enumerate(docs):
            for w in doc.split():
                if w in self.vocab:                      # unseen words carry no evidence either way
                    X[r, self.vocab[w]] += 1
        return X

    def predict_log_proba(self, docs):
        joint = self._counts(docs) @ self.log_lik.T + self.log_prior       # log P(c) + Σ n_w log P(w|c)
        return joint - np.logaddexp.reduce(joint, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # normalise in log space

    def predict(self, docs):
        return [self.classes[i] for i in self.predict_log_proba(docs).argmax(1)]

Check it

Work one posterior out by hand, then test the edge cases the log-space design exists for.

docs = ["win cash now", "win prize now", "meeting at noon", "lunch at noon"]
labels = ["spam", "spam", "ham", "ham"]
nb = MultinomialNB().fit(docs, labels)

# by hand: vocabulary of 8 words, 6 word tokens per class.
# P(win|spam) = (2+1)/(6+8) = 3/14, P(win|ham) = (0+1)/(6+8) = 1/14, equal priors
# => P(spam | "win") = 3 / (3 + 1) = 0.75
p = np.exp(nb.predict_log_proba(["win"]))[0]
assert np.isclose(p[nb.classes.index("spam")], 0.75)

assert nb.predict(["win a prize", "lunch meeting"]) == ["spam", "ham"]
assert np.allclose(np.exp(nb.predict_log_proba(docs)).sum(1), 1.0)   # rows are distributions

# an unseen word changes nothing; an empty document returns the prior
assert np.allclose(nb.predict_log_proba(["win zebra"]), nb.predict_log_proba(["win"]))
assert np.allclose(nb.predict_log_proba([""])[0], nb.log_prior)

# 5,000 words: the probability product underflows, the log-space sum does not
long_doc = " ".join(["noon"] * 5000)
assert np.prod(np.exp(nb.log_lik[nb.classes.index("ham")][nb.vocab["noon"]]) * np.ones(5000)) == 0.0
lp = nb.predict_log_proba([long_doc])
assert np.isfinite(lp).all() and nb.predict([long_doc]) == ["ham"]

Complexity

Training is one pass over the tokens, O(total tokens), plus O(K·V) for the table. Prediction is O(tokens in the document × K) — with a sparse document matrix the dense (n, V) array above disappears.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Log space end to end, including the normalisation: logaddexp.reduce is log-sum-exp, so the posterior never leaves log space.
  • Smoothing denominator includes α·V — the most common bug is adding α to the numerator only, which makes the “probabilities” not sum to 1.
  • Unseen words at test time are dropped. Scoring them with the smoothed probability α/(total_c + αV) would add a penalty that is larger for classes with more training text, quietly biasing predictions toward the smaller classes.
  • A hand-computed posterior in the test is the fastest way to prove the arithmetic, and interviewers notice when you do it.
deep:
Why NB works despite the false assumption

  • Words are obviously not independent. The consequence is that correlated evidence is counted several times, which pushes posteriors toward 0 and 1 — NB is badly calibrated. But classification only needs the argmax to be right, and the ranking is often good. Domingos and Pazzani showed NB can be optimal under 0-1 loss even with strong dependencies.
  • If you need probabilities (for thresholds or downstream decisions), calibrate on held-out data with Platt scaling or isotonic regression.

Variants

  • Bernoulli NB models presence/absence and penalises absent words — better for short texts.
  • Complement NB estimates parameters from all classes except c, which is more stable for imbalanced classes (Rennie et al., 2003).
  • Gaussian NB for continuous features: each feature is a per-class normal distribution.
  • TF-IDF and length normalisation reduce the dominance of long documents and bursty words, fixing some of NB's systematic errors.

Generative vs discriminative

NB is the generative partner of logistic regression: same linear decision boundary in log space, but NB estimates P(x | y) and inverts it, while logistic regression fits P(y | x) directly. Ng and Jordan (2001) showed NB reaches its (higher) asymptotic error with far fewer examples — so NB wins with little data and logistic regression wins with a lot.
drill:
Work it out

Implement Gaussian Naive Bayes for continuous features: per class, fit a mean and variance for each feature, and classify with the sum of per-feature log densities. Why does scikit-learn add a small var_smoothing term?

Answer 
class GaussianNB:
    def __init__(self, var_smoothing=1e-9):
        self.var_smoothing = var_smoothing

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.classes = np.unique(y)
        eps = self.var_smoothing * X.var(0).max()          # guards against zero variance
        self.mu = np.array([X[y == c].mean(0) for c in self.classes])
        self.var = np.array([X[y == c].var(0) + eps for c in self.classes])
        self.log_prior = np.log(np.array([(y == c).mean() for c in self.classes]))
        return self

    def predict_log_proba(self, X):
        ll = -0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi * self.var)[None] + (X[:, None, :] - self.mu[None]) ** 2 / self.var[None]).sum(-1)
        joint = ll + self.log_prior
        return joint - np.logaddexp.reduce(joint, axis=1, keepdims=True)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xg = np.vstack([rng.normal([0, 0], 1, (200, 2)), rng.normal([3, 3], 1, (200, 2))])
yg = np.repeat([0, 1], 200)
g = GaussianNB().fit(Xg, yg)
assert (g.predict_log_proba(Xg).argmax(1) == yg).mean() > 0.95

Xz = np.c_[Xg, np.ones(400)]                    # a constant feature has variance exactly 0
assert np.isfinite(GaussianNB().fit(Xz, yg).predict_log_proba(Xz)).all()

A feature that is constant within a class has zero variance, and the Gaussian log-density then divides by zero. var_smoothing adds a tiny fraction of the largest feature variance to every variance — the continuous-feature analogue of Laplace smoothing.
qa: E
What is 'naive' about Naive Bayes?

It assumes features are conditionally independent given the class, so the class-conditional likelihood factorises into a product of per-feature terms. That makes training a matter of counting, at the cost of double-counting correlated evidence.
M
Why compute Naive Bayes in log space?

The likelihood is a product of many small probabilities, which underflows to exactly 0 in floating point for documents of a few hundred words. Summing log-probabilities avoids it, and normalising with log-sum-exp keeps the posterior in log space too.
M
What problem does Laplace smoothing solve?

A word never seen with a class gets probability 0, which zeroes the whole product regardless of all other evidence. Adding α to every count (and α·V to the denominator) gives unseen words a small non-zero probability; α acts as a symmetric Dirichlet prior.
H
Naive Bayes probabilities are poorly calibrated but its accuracy is often fine. Why?

Correlated features are counted as independent evidence, which pushes posteriors toward 0 and 1 — overconfidence. The argmax can still be right because the errors often preserve the ranking; NB can be optimal under 0-1 loss even with dependencies. If you need probabilities, calibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data.

sum: Centre, decompose, project — and why the SVD of X beats the eigendecomposition of its covariance.
primer:
What PCA finds

Principal component analysis finds the directions along which the data vary most. The first component is the unit vector that maximises the variance of the data projected onto it; each later component does the same while staying orthogonal to the earlier ones. Keeping the top k gives the best k-dimensional linear approximation of the data in squared error.

Two routes to the same answer

  • Eigendecomposition of the covariance matrix Σ = XcᵀXc/(n − 1): the eigenvectors are the components, the eigenvalues are the variances along them.
  • SVD of the centred data Xc = U·S·Vᵀ: the rows of Vᵀ are the same components, and s²/(n − 1) are the same variances. This route never forms XᵀX, which squares the condition number and loses precision.

The vocabulary

  • Components / loadings — the directions (k × d).
  • Scores — the data expressed in the new coordinates (n × k).
  • Explained variance ratio — each component's share of the total variance; choose k to keep, say, 95%.
  • Reconstruction — map scores back: X̂ = scores·components + mean.

Two things people forget

Centre the data first (otherwise the first component points at the mean), and standardise when features are in different units (otherwise the component just follows whichever feature has the largest numbers).
body:
The problem

“Implement PCA with fit, transform and inverse_transform, and report the explained variance ratio.” Clarify whether to standardise, and how many components to keep.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

class PCA:
    def __init__(self, n_components):
        self.k = n_components

    def fit(self, X):
        X = np.asarray(X, float)
        self.mean = X.mean(0)
        U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X - self.mean, full_matrices=False)
        # singular vectors have an arbitrary sign; fix it so results are reproducible
        signs = np.sign(Vt[np.arange(len(Vt)), np.abs(Vt).argmax(1)])
        Vt = Vt * signs[:, None]
        var = S ** 2 / (len(X) - 1)                       # variance along each component
        self.components = Vt[:self.k]                      # (k, d), orthonormal rows
        self.explained_variance = var[:self.k]
        self.explained_variance_ratio = var[:self.k] / var.sum()
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return (np.asarray(X, float) - self.mean) @ self.components.T     # (n, k) scores

    def inverse_transform(self, Z):
        return Z @ self.components + self.mean

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# 500 points that really live on a 2-D plane inside 5-D space, plus a little noise
basis = np.linalg.qr(rng.normal(size=(5, 2)))[0].T            # (2, 5) orthonormal
X = rng.normal(size=(500, 2)) * [5.0, 2.0] @ basis + 0.01 * rng.normal(size=(500, 5)) + 3.0

p = PCA(2).fit(X)
assert np.allclose(p.components @ p.components.T, np.eye(2))            # orthonormal
assert p.explained_variance_ratio.sum() > 0.999                          # two components suffice
assert np.abs(p.inverse_transform(p.transform(X)) - X).max() < 0.1      # near-perfect reconstruction

# same answer as the eigendecomposition of the covariance
evals, evecs = np.linalg.eigh(np.cov(X, rowvar=False))
assert np.allclose(np.sort(evals)[::-1][:2], p.explained_variance)
assert np.allclose(np.abs(evecs[:, ::-1][:, :2].T @ p.components.T), np.eye(2), atol=1e-6)

# the variance of the scores along each component is the explained variance
assert np.allclose(p.transform(X).var(0, ddof=1), p.explained_variance)

Complexity

A thin SVD of an n × d matrix costs O(n·d·min(n, d)). The covariance route is O(n·d²) to form Σ plus O(d³) to decompose it — similar cost, worse numerics. For only the top k of a large matrix, randomised SVD costs about O(n·d·k).

Details that separate a good answer

  • Centre, and say whether you standardise. PCA on raw features in different units measures units, not structure.
  • Fix the sign of each component. The SVD is unique only up to sign, so two runs or two libraries can return mirrored components; downstream code comparing them will break without a convention.
  • ddof = 1 — the sample variance divides by n − 1, and the test checks that the scores' variance matches.
  • Verify against eigh, comparing up to sign — a second route to the same answer is the strongest test.
deep:
Scaling PCA up

  • Randomised SVD (Halko, Martinsson, Tropp): multiply X by a random d × (k + p) matrix, orthonormalise the result, and do an exact SVD in that small subspace. A few power iterations make it accurate when the spectrum decays slowly. This is scikit-learn's default for large inputs.
  • Sparse data: centring destroys sparsity. Either use TruncatedSVD (no centring — this is LSA for text) or apply the centring implicitly inside the matrix–vector products.
  • Streaming: incremental PCA updates the decomposition batch by batch; or accumulate XᵀX and the mean in one pass if d is moderate.

What PCA is and is not

  • It is the optimal linear autoencoder: a linear encoder/decoder trained on squared error spans the same subspace.
  • It is unsupervised — the high-variance directions need not be the predictive ones. Using PCA before a classifier can throw away exactly the small-variance direction that separates the classes.
  • It captures linear structure only. Kernel PCA, t-SNE and UMAP handle curved manifolds; t-SNE and UMAP are for visualisation — distances between clusters in their plots are not meaningful.
  • Whitening (divide scores by √variance) gives unit-variance, uncorrelated features; it amplifies noise in the low-variance directions.

Where it shows up in AI systems

Reducing embedding dimension before indexing, visualising embedding drift, the first step of product quantisation (rotating so variance is balanced across subspaces), and inspecting activation spaces in interpretability work.
drill:
Work it out

Show that the reconstruction error of a k-component PCA equals the sum of the variances of the discarded components. Then write a function that picks the smallest k keeping at least 95% of the variance.

Answer

Because the components are orthonormal, the centred data split into two orthogonal parts: the projection onto the kept components and the residual in the discarded ones. The squared error of the reconstruction is exactly the residual's squared norm, which is the sum of the discarded s². Divide by n − 1 and it is the sum of the discarded variances (the discarded eigenvalues).

def k_for_variance(X, keep=0.95):
    full = PCA(min(X.shape)).fit(X)
    return int(np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(full.explained_variance_ratio), keep) + 1)

Xw = rng.normal(size=(300, 6)) * [6, 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.1]
full = PCA(6).fit(Xw)
for k in range(1, 6):
    pk = PCA(k).fit(Xw)
    err = ((Xw - pk.inverse_transform(pk.transform(Xw))) ** 2).sum() / (len(Xw) - 1)
    assert np.isclose(err, full.explained_variance[k:].sum())

k = k_for_variance(Xw)
assert np.cumsum(full.explained_variance_ratio)[k - 1] >= 0.95 > np.cumsum(full.explained_variance_ratio)[k - 2]

The identity is also why the explained-variance curve is the right tool for choosing k: the variance you drop is the squared reconstruction error you accept.
qa: E
Why must the data be centred before PCA?

PCA finds directions of maximum variance about the mean. Without centring, the SVD finds directions of maximum second moment about the origin, so the first component points toward the mean of the data rather than along its spread.
M
Why compute PCA from the SVD of X rather than the eigendecomposition of the covariance?

Forming XᵀX squares the condition number, so small eigenvalues lose precision or become negative through rounding. The SVD works on X directly and is backward stable. Both give the same components and variances in exact arithmetic.
M
When should features be standardised before PCA?

When they are in different units or have very different scales, otherwise the first components simply follow the features with the largest numeric variance. If all features share a unit and their scale is meaningful (pixel intensities, embedding coordinates), leave them unscaled.
H
How would you run PCA on a 10 million × 100,000 sparse matrix?

Do not densify or explicitly centre it. Use randomised SVD or Lanczos with the centring applied implicitly inside matrix–vector products (or skip centring and use TruncatedSVD if that is acceptable). Only the top k components are needed, so cost is about O(nnz·k) per pass.
