t: Scaled dot-product and multi-head attention with masks
sum: The most-asked LLM coding question: attention in NumPy, head splitting by reshape, causal and padding masks.
primer:
Attention in one paragraph

Each token produces three vectors: a query (what am I looking for?), a key (what do I contain?) and a value (what do I pass on if chosen?). A token's output is a weighted average of all the values, where the weights come from how well its query matches each key: softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k)·V.

Shapes, said out loud

  • Q (T, d_k), K (T, d_k), V (T, d_v) for a sequence of T tokens.
  • QKᵀ is (T, T): row i scores token i's query against every key.
  • Softmax over each row turns scores into weights that sum to 1; multiplying by V gives (T, d_v).

Why divide by √d_k

A dot product of two random vectors with unit-variance entries has variance d_k. With d_k = 128, scores have a standard deviation around 11, softmax saturates to nearly one-hot, and its gradient vanishes. Dividing by √d_k brings the variance back to 1.

Masks

  • Causal mask: in a decoder, token i may only attend to tokens 0…i. Set the scores above the diagonal to −∞ before the softmax, so their weights are exactly 0.
  • Padding mask: in a batch of different-length sequences, pad tokens must not be attended to.

Multi-head attention

Instead of one attention with d_model-sized vectors, split into h heads of size d_model / h, run attention in each independently, concatenate and project. Different heads learn different relations (syntax, coreference, position). The split is just a reshape and a transpose — no loop over heads.
body:
The problem

“Implement scaled dot-product attention and multi-head self-attention in NumPy, with a causal mask.” Clarify: batch dimension, mask convention (True = may attend), and whether dropout is needed (no, for inference).

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    """Q (..., Tq, dk), K (..., Tk, dk), V (..., Tk, dv); mask broadcastable to (..., Tq, Tk), True = may attend."""
    scores = Q @ np.swapaxes(K, -1, -2) / np.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])      # (..., Tq, Tk)
    if mask is not None:
        # a large finite negative, not -inf: a fully masked row then gives uniform weights, not NaN
        scores = np.where(mask, scores, np.finfo(scores.dtype).min)
    weights = softmax(scores)
    return weights @ V, weights

def causal_mask(T):
    return np.tril(np.ones((T, T), dtype=bool))                        # row i may see columns 0..i

class MultiHeadAttention:
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, seed=0):
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.h, self.dk = n_heads, d_model // n_heads
        std = 1 / np.sqrt(d_model)
        self.Wq, self.Wk, self.Wv, self.Wo = (rng.normal(0, std, (d_model, d_model)) for _ in range(4))

    def split(self, x):                                   # (B, T, D) -> (B, h, T, dk)
        B, T, _ = x.shape
        return x.reshape(B, T, self.h, self.dk).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)

    def __call__(self, x, mask=None):
        B, T, D = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.split(x @ self.Wq), self.split(x @ self.Wk), self.split(x @ self.Wv)
        out, w = attention(q, k, v, mask)                  # all heads at once: (B, h, T, dk)
        out = out.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(B, T, D)   # concatenate the heads
        return out @ self.Wo, w

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
B, T, D, H = 2, 6, 16, 4
x = rng.normal(size=(B, T, D))
mha = MultiHeadAttention(D, H)
out, w = mha(x, causal_mask(T))
assert out.shape == (B, T, D) and w.shape == (B, H, T, T)
assert np.allclose(w.sum(-1), 1) and np.all(np.triu(w[0, 0], k=1) == 0)   # no weight on the future

# causality: changing future tokens never changes earlier outputs
x2 = x.copy(); x2[:, 4:] = rng.normal(size=(B, 2, D))
assert np.allclose(mha(x2, causal_mask(T))[0][:, :4], out[:, :4])

# the reshape trick equals an explicit loop over heads
heads = []
for i in range(H):
    s = slice(i * mha.dk, (i + 1) * mha.dk)
    o, _ = attention(x @ mha.Wq[:, s], x @ mha.Wk[:, s], x @ mha.Wv[:, s], causal_mask(T))
    heads.append(o)
assert np.allclose(np.concatenate(heads, -1) @ mha.Wo, out)

# without a mask or positions, attention is permutation-equivariant
perm = rng.permutation(T)
assert np.allclose(mha(x[:, perm])[0], mha(x)[0][:, perm])

Complexity

  • Time: O(T²·d) for the scores and the weighted sum, plus O(T·d²) for the four projections. The projections dominate for short sequences, the T² term for long ones.
  • Memory: the (B, h, T, T) weight tensor. At T = 32k that is 4 GB per head per sequence in fp32 — the reason FlashAttention exists.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Say the shapes at every line; interviewers follow along by shape.
  • Mask before softmax, with a large negative rather than −inf if any row could be fully masked (padding), otherwise that row becomes NaN and poisons the batch.
  • Heads by reshape, not a Python loop — and prove the equivalence, as the test does.
  • Know the permutation property: attention has no notion of order, which is why positional information must be added (the next problem).
deep:
What changes in production attention

  • Fused QKV: one (D, 3D) matmul instead of three, then split — fewer kernel launches.
  • FlashAttention: computes exactly the same result without materialising the T × T matrix, tiling Q, K and V through on-chip SRAM and using an online softmax (running max and sum). Memory becomes O(T); FLOPs stay O(T²); wall-clock drops because the bottleneck was memory traffic, not arithmetic.
  • Grouped-query attention: n_kv < n_heads key/value heads, each shared by a group of query heads. In code, project K and V to n_kv·d_k, then broadcast each KV head across its group (repeat or a reshape to (B, n_kv, group, T, d_k)). The KV cache shrinks by n_heads / n_kv.
  • Multi-head latent attention (DeepSeek-V2/V3) caches a low-rank latent instead of full K and V, shrinking the cache further.

Numerics

  • In fp16/bf16, compute the softmax in fp32 or with the max-subtraction — scores can exceed the fp16 range for long sequences.
  • Some models add QK-norm (normalising queries and keys) or logit soft-capping (Gemma 2) to stop attention logits growing during training.
  • Attention sinks: many heads put large weight on the first token as a “no-op” target. Streaming inference must keep those first tokens in the cache or quality collapses.

Variants you may be asked to modify the code for

  • Cross-attention: queries from the decoder, keys/values from the encoder — only the inputs to the projections change.
  • Sliding-window attention: a band mask; with W-token windows memory is O(T·W).
  • ALiBi: add a head-specific linear penalty −m·|i − j| to the scores instead of positional embeddings.
drill:
Work it out

A batch holds sequences of lengths 6 and 3, padded to 6. Build a mask combining the causal mask and a key-padding mask, and show that the outputs for the real tokens of the short sequence equal what you get by running it alone, unpadded.

Answer

The key-padding mask has shape (B, 1, 1, T) — broadcast over heads and query positions — and the causal mask (T, T). Their logical AND broadcasts to (B, 1, T, T). Pad queries produce garbage outputs, which is fine: the loss and every later layer ignore them.

lengths = np.array([6, 3])
x = rng.normal(size=(2, T, D))
key_ok = np.arange(T)[None, :] < lengths[:, None]                  # (B, T): real tokens
mask = causal_mask(T)[None, None] & key_ok[:, None, None, :]        # (B, 1, T, T)
out, w = mha(x, mask)

alone, _ = mha(x[1:2, :3], causal_mask(3))                          # the short sequence, unpadded
assert np.allclose(out[1, :3], alone[0])
assert np.all(w[1][..., 3:] == 0)                                   # no weight on pad keys

With right padding, the causal mask already prevents real tokens from seeing the pads that come after them, so the padding mask matters most for left padding (used for batched generation) and for bidirectional encoders. Say that, and note that pad positions must also be excluded from the loss with ignore_index.
qa: E
Why divide the attention scores by √d_k?

A dot product of two d_k-dimensional vectors with unit-variance entries has variance d_k. Without scaling, large d_k produces large scores that saturate the softmax to nearly one-hot, where gradients vanish. Dividing by √d_k restores unit variance.
M
What are the time and memory costs of self-attention?

O(T²·d) time for QKᵀ and the weighted sum, plus O(T·d²) for the projections, and O(T²) memory per head for the weight matrix. FlashAttention keeps the O(T²) FLOPs but cuts memory to O(T) by never materialising the matrix.
M
Why is attention permutation-equivariant, and what fixes it?

Every token attends to every key with weights that depend only on content, so permuting the inputs permutes the outputs identically — the model cannot tell order. Positional information fixes it: added embeddings (sinusoidal, learned), rotations of Q and K (RoPE) or score biases (ALiBi).
H
How would you change this implementation for grouped-query attention?

Project K and V to n_kv heads instead of n_heads, then broadcast each KV head across its group of n_heads/n_kv query heads (repeat along the head axis or reshape queries to (B, n_kv, group, T, d_k)). Outputs keep the same shape; the KV cache and K/V projection cost shrink by n_heads/n_kv.

sum: Build both, then prove RoPE's defining property: the query–key score depends only on the distance between positions.
primer:
Why position has to be added

Attention treats its input as a set: shuffle the tokens and each output is shuffled the same way. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” would look identical. Positional encoding injects order.

Sinusoidal encodings (the original Transformer)

Add to each token embedding a fixed vector whose pairs of dimensions are sin and cos of the position at geometrically spaced frequencies: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d)), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(…). Fast frequencies distinguish neighbours; slow ones distinguish distant positions. Moving by k positions is a fixed rotation of each (sin, cos) pair, so relative offsets are easy for the model to read.

RoPE — rotary position embedding (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, almost every current LLM)

Instead of adding a vector, rotate the query and key. Treat each pair of dimensions as a 2-D point and rotate it by angle pos·θ_i, with the same geometric frequencies. Because rotating q by angle a and k by angle b changes their dot product only through a − b, the attention score depends on the relative position m − n, never the absolute ones. Values are not rotated — position only affects who attends to whom, not what is passed.

Why it matters for interviews

RoPE is the mechanism behind every context-extension trick (position interpolation, NTK scaling, YaRN), and “implement RoPE” is a common LLM coding question precisely because the relative-position property can be tested in three lines.
body:
The problem

“Implement sinusoidal positional encodings and RoPE. Show that RoPE makes the attention score depend only on relative position.” Clarify the pairing convention: adjacent dimensions (the paper) or first half with second half (the Hugging Face LLaMA code) — they are equivalent up to a fixed permutation of dimensions, but checkpoints are not interchangeable between them.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def sinusoidal(T, d, base=10000.0):
    pos = np.arange(T)[:, None]
    freq = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)          # (d/2,) geometric frequencies
    pe = np.zeros((T, d))
    pe[:, 0::2], pe[:, 1::2] = np.sin(pos * freq), np.cos(pos * freq)
    return pe

def rope_angles(T, dk, base=10000.0, offset=0, scale=1.0):
    """Angle for every (position, pair): (T, dk/2). `scale` < 1 is position interpolation."""
    inv_freq = base ** (-np.arange(0, dk, 2) / dk)
    return np.outer((np.arange(offset, offset + T)) * scale, inv_freq)

def apply_rope(x, angles):
    """Rotate each adjacent pair (x[2i], x[2i+1]) of the last axis by its angle. x (..., T, dk)."""
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    cos, sin = np.cos(angles), np.sin(angles)
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2] = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    out[..., 1::2] = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return out

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
dk, T = 64, 32
q, k = rng.normal(size=dk), rng.normal(size=dk)
A = rope_angles(T, dk)

def score(m, n):                     # q at position m attends to k at position n
    return apply_rope(q[None], A[m:m + 1])[0] @ apply_rope(k[None], A[n:n + 1])[0]

# the defining property: only the offset m - n matters
assert np.isclose(score(5, 2), score(13, 10)) and np.isclose(score(7, 7), score(0, 0))
assert np.isclose(score(0, 0), q @ k)                  # position 0 is no rotation
assert not np.isclose(score(5, 2), score(2, 5))        # but direction matters

# rotation preserves length, so RoPE never changes a vector's norm
X = rng.normal(size=(T, dk))
assert np.allclose(np.linalg.norm(apply_rope(X, A), axis=-1), np.linalg.norm(X, axis=-1))

# incremental decoding: rotating the token at position 20 alone equals slicing the full result
assert np.allclose(apply_rope(X[20:21], rope_angles(1, dk, offset=20)), apply_rope(X, A)[20:21])

# sinusoidal: shifting by k positions is a fixed rotation of each (sin, cos) pair
pe = sinusoidal(50, 16)
freq = 10000.0 ** (-np.arange(0, 16, 2) / 16)
kk = 7
for i, w in enumerate(freq):
    R = np.array([[np.cos(kk * w), -np.sin(kk * w)], [np.sin(kk * w), np.cos(kk * w)]])
    assert np.allclose(pe[:40, 2 * i:2 * i + 2] @ R, pe[kk:40 + kk, 2 * i:2 * i + 2])

Complexity

O(T·d) element-wise work for either scheme; the angles (or their cos/sin) are precomputed once per maximum length and cached.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Apply RoPE to Q and K after projection, not to V and not to the residual stream.
  • The offset: during cached decoding, the new token's rotation uses its absolute position (offset = tokens so far). Forgetting it is the classic KV-cache bug — generation still “works” but degrades.
  • Test the property, not the formula: score(m, n) == score(m + c, n + c) is a better test than comparing to a hand-computed rotation.
  • Name the convention (interleaved vs half-split) — mixing them when loading weights is a real bug that produces fluent nonsense.
deep:
Context extension, mechanically

  • A model trained to length L has only seen angles up to L·θ_i for each frequency. Beyond L, the slow dimensions produce unseen angles and attention degrades sharply.
  • Position interpolation (PI): multiply positions by L / L′ so the new length maps into the trained range. Works with light fine-tuning, but squeezes the fast frequencies too, blurring local order.
  • NTK-aware scaling: raise the base (base′ = base·s^(d/(d−2))) so fast frequencies are nearly unchanged and slow ones are interpolated — some extension even without fine-tuning.
  • YaRN: interpolate per frequency band (leave high frequencies, interpolate low, blend between) and add a temperature to the attention logits. Used by many open long-context models.
  • Base choice: long-context models ship with much larger bases (LLaMA 3 uses 500,000) so that slow frequencies still vary slowly at 128k tokens.

Alternatives and their trade-offs

  • Learned absolute embeddings (GPT-2, BERT): simple, cannot extrapolate beyond the trained length at all.
  • ALiBi: no embeddings; a head-specific linear penalty on distance added to the scores. Extrapolates gracefully, but is less used in frontier models.
  • NoPE: causal decoders can infer position from the causal mask alone — works surprisingly well at small scale.
  • Partial RoPE: rotate only a fraction of each head's dimensions (some models) or decouple a small RoPE component from the cached latent (DeepSeek's MLA).

An insight worth stating

Because RoPE's frequencies are geometric, each pair of dimensions acts like a clock hand at a different speed. The model reads relative position from how far each hand has turned between query and key — the same idea as a binary counter, but smooth.
drill:
Work it out

A model was trained with RoPE to 4,096 tokens and you need 16,384. Implement position interpolation and NTK-aware base scaling, and check how each changes the angles of the fastest and slowest frequency pairs at position 16,383.

Answer 
L, L_new, dk, base = 4096, 16384, 128, 10000.0
s = L_new / L
edge = rope_angles(1, dk, offset=L)[0]                         # training covered angles below this, per pair

pi = rope_angles(1, dk, offset=L_new - 1, scale=1 / s)[0]     # squeeze positions into [0, L)
ntk = rope_angles(1, dk, base=base * s ** (dk / (dk - 2)), offset=L_new - 1)[0]
plain = rope_angles(1, dk, offset=L_new - 1)[0]

assert np.all(pi < edge)                                        # PI: every angle is in the trained range
assert plain[-1] > 3 * edge[-1]                                 # unscaled: slowest pair far out of range
assert np.isclose(ntk[-1], edge[-1], rtol=0.01)                 # NTK: slowest pair lands at the trained edge
assert np.isclose(ntk[0], plain[0]) and not np.isclose(pi[0], plain[0])   # NTK leaves the fastest pair alone

PI shrinks every frequency by 4×, so neighbouring tokens become 4× harder to tell apart — hence the fine-tuning it needs. NTK scaling changes the base so the slowest pair is exactly interpolated while the fastest pair is untouched, preserving local resolution; intermediate frequencies get intermediate treatment. YaRN makes that blend explicit per band and adds an attention temperature.

Why do transformers need positional information at all?

Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: without positions the model sees a bag of tokens and cannot distinguish 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'. Positional encodings or position-dependent attention biases break that symmetry.
M
What property makes RoPE a relative position encoding?

Queries and keys are rotated by angles proportional to their positions, and the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the difference of the rotation angles. So the score between position m and n depends on m − n, while each vector's norm is unchanged.
M
Why is RoPE applied to queries and keys but not values?

Position should influence which tokens attend to which — that is decided by the QK scores. Values carry the content that is mixed; rotating them would inject absolute-position artefacts into the output without helping the relative-position matching.
H
How do position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN differ?

PI multiplies positions by L/L′ so all angles stay in the trained range, but compresses high frequencies and blurs local order, so it needs fine-tuning. NTK-aware scaling raises the base, leaving high frequencies nearly unchanged and interpolating low ones. YaRN interpolates per frequency band with a smooth ramp and adds an attention temperature, extending further with little fine-tuning.

t: A GPT-style decoder and generation with a KV cache
sum: Pre-norm blocks, weight tying, prefill then one-token decode steps — and a test that the cache changes nothing but speed.
primer:
The decoder block

A GPT-style model is a stack of identical blocks on a residual stream. Each block does two things, each wrapped as x = x + f(norm(x)) (pre-norm):

  1. Causal self-attention — tokens exchange information, each looking only backwards.
  2. MLP — each token is processed on its own: expand to 4·d, apply a nonlinearity (GELU or SwiGLU), project back.

Token embeddings go in at the bottom; a final norm and a projection to vocabulary logits come out at the top. Many models tie the output projection to the input embedding matrix, saving V·d parameters.

Why generation needs a cache

To generate token 101, the model needs keys and values for tokens 1–100 at every layer. Because of the causal mask, those never change once computed — later tokens cannot affect earlier ones. So store them. Generation then has two phases:

  • Prefill: run the whole prompt in one parallel pass, filling the cache. Sets the time to first token.
  • Decode: feed only the newest token; compute its query, key and value, append the key and value to the cache, attend over the cache. One token per step.

Without the cache, step t redoes t tokens of work, so generating n tokens costs O(n²) token-passes instead of O(n).
body:
The problem

“Implement a tiny GPT forward pass and greedy generation, with and without a KV cache. Show that both produce identical tokens.” This combines the attention and positional problems with the one detail everyone gets wrong: the causal mask when queries and keys have different lengths.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def softmax(z):
    z = z - z.max(-1, keepdims=True); e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True)

def rms_norm(x, g, eps=1e-6):
    return g * x / np.sqrt((x * x).mean(-1, keepdims=True) + eps)

def gelu(x):
    return 0.5 * x * (1 + np.tanh(np.sqrt(2 / np.pi) * (x + 0.044715 * x ** 3)))

class TinyGPT:
    def __init__(self, vocab, d=32, n_heads=4, n_layers=2, max_T=64, seed=0):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        init = lambda *shape: rng.normal(0, 0.1, shape)
        self.h, self.dk = n_heads, d // n_heads
        self.tok, self.pos = init(vocab, d), init(max_T, d)
        self.layers = [dict(g1=np.ones(d), Wqkv=init(d, 3 * d), Wo=init(d, d),
                            g2=np.ones(d), W1=init(d, 4 * d), W2=init(4 * d, d)) for _ in range(n_layers)]
        self.g_final = np.ones(d)

    def attn(self, L, x, cache):
        T, D = x.shape
        q, k, v = np.split(x @ L["Wqkv"], 3, axis=-1)
        heads = lambda t: t.reshape(T, self.h, self.dk).transpose(1, 0, 2)      # (h, T, dk)
        q, k, v = heads(q), heads(k), heads(v)
        if cache is not None:
            if "k" in cache:                                   # append to what earlier steps stored
                k = np.concatenate([cache["k"], k], axis=1)
                v = np.concatenate([cache["v"], v], axis=1)
            cache["k"], cache["v"] = k, v
        S = k.shape[1]                                         # keys available: past + new
        scores = q @ k.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(self.dk)   # (h, T, S)
        # new query t sits at absolute position S - T + t and may see keys 0 .. S - T + t
        allowed = np.arange(S)[None, :] <= (S - T + np.arange(T))[:, None]
        scores = np.where(allowed, scores, -np.inf)
        return (softmax(scores) @ v).transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, D) @ L["Wo"]

    def forward(self, ids, caches=None, start=0):
        x = self.tok[ids] + self.pos[start:start + len(ids)]
        for i, L in enumerate(self.layers):
            x = x + self.attn(L, rms_norm(x, L["g1"]), None if caches is None else caches[i])
            x = x + gelu(rms_norm(x, L["g2"]) @ L["W1"]) @ L["W2"]
        return rms_norm(x, self.g_final) @ self.tok.T          # weight tying: logits (T, vocab)

    def generate(self, prompt, n_new, use_cache=True):
        ids = list(prompt)
        if not use_cache:
            for _ in range(n_new):                             # recompute everything every step
                ids.append(int(self.forward(np.array(ids))[-1].argmax()))
            return ids
        caches = [{} for _ in self.layers]
        logits = self.forward(np.array(ids), caches)           # prefill: the whole prompt at once
        for step in range(n_new):
            ids.append(int(logits[-1].argmax()))
            if step < n_new - 1:                               # decode: one new token per step
                logits = self.forward(np.array(ids[-1:]), caches, start=len(ids) - 1)
        return ids

Check it

model = TinyGPT(vocab=50)
prompt = [3, 14, 15, 9, 2, 6]
assert model.generate(prompt, 20) == model.generate(prompt, 20, use_cache=False)

# step by step: each cached decode step reproduces the last row of a full forward pass
ids = list(prompt)
caches = [{} for _ in model.layers]
model.forward(np.array(ids), caches)
for tok in [7, 1, 8]:
    ids.append(tok)
    step_logits = model.forward(np.array([tok]), caches, start=len(ids) - 1)[-1]
    assert np.allclose(step_logits, model.forward(np.array(ids))[-1])
assert caches[0]["k"].shape == (model.h, len(ids), model.dk)     # the cache grows by one per step

# chunked prefill (prompt in two pieces) matches a single prefill
c1 = [{} for _ in model.layers]
model.forward(np.array(prompt[:4]), c1)
chunked = model.forward(np.array(prompt[4:]), c1, start=4)[-1]
assert np.allclose(chunked, model.forward(np.array(prompt))[-1])

Complexity

  • Without a cache: generating n tokens after a prompt of p runs the model over p, p+1, …, p+n−1 tokens — O(n·(p + n)) token-passes, and quadratic attention inside each.
  • With a cache: one pass over p tokens, then n single-token passes, each attending over the cache — linear in the number of tokens processed.
  • Cache memory: 2 × layers × heads × d_k × tokens numbers per sequence, and it grows with every generated token.

Details that separate a good answer

  • The mask when T ≠ S: a new query at absolute position S − T + t sees all keys up to itself. Using tril(ones(T, S)) is the classic bug — it masks the cache instead of the future. The chunked-prefill test catches it.
  • Positions continue from where the cache ends (start), or position embeddings/RoPE are applied at the wrong offset.
  • Test equivalence exactly: the cache is an optimisation, so cached and uncached generation must produce the same tokens and the same logits.
  • Pre-norm keeps an un-normalised residual path, which is why the final norm before the output projection is required.
deep:
Why decode is slow, in one calculation

At batch size 1, every decode step reads all the weights from GPU memory to produce one token. A 70B model in fp16 is 140 GB; at 3.35 TB/s (H100) that is ~42 ms per token no matter how many FLOPs the chip has. Decoding is memory-bandwidth bound; batching many sequences amortises each weight read over many tokens until compute or KV-cache memory becomes the limit. Prefill processes many tokens per weight read and is compute bound.

Production KV-cache engineering

  • PagedAttention (vLLM): store the cache in fixed-size blocks mapped through a block table, like virtual memory — no fragmentation, and blocks can be shared copy-on-write between sequences with a common prefix or between parallel samples.
  • Prefix caching: reuse the cache for a shared system prompt across requests; providers expose it as cheaper “cached input tokens”.
  • Chunked prefill: split long prompts into chunks interleaved with decode steps so one long prompt does not stall everyone else's tokens — the test above shows why it is exact.
  • Shrinking the cache: GQA/MQA (fewer KV heads), MLA (low-rank latent), KV quantisation to fp8/int4, sliding-window layers, and eviction policies that keep attention sinks plus recent tokens.
  • Disaggregation: run prefill and decode on different GPU pools and ship the cache between them, because they have opposite bottlenecks.

Batched generation details

Real servers batch sequences of different lengths: left-padding with an attention mask and per-sequence position ids in simple implementations, or ragged per-sequence caches with continuous batching (new requests join the batch at any decode step) in serving engines.

Work it out

Write a function for the KV-cache size and use it for Llama-3-8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, bf16). How much cache does one 8,192-token conversation need, and how many such conversations fit in the 40 GB left on an 80 GB GPU after the weights? What if the model used 32 KV heads (no GQA)?

Answer 
def kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, tokens, bytes_per_value=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * tokens * bytes_per_value      # 2 = keys and values

per_token = kv_cache_bytes(32, 8, 128, 1)
per_conv = kv_cache_bytes(32, 8, 128, 8192)
assert per_token == 131_072                        # 128 KiB per token
assert per_conv == 1024 ** 3                       # exactly 1 GiB per 8k-token conversation
assert int(40e9 // per_conv) == 37                 # ~37 concurrent 8k conversations
assert kv_cache_bytes(32, 32, 128, 8192) == 4 * per_conv    # without GQA: 4 GiB each, ~9 fit

128 KiB per token, 1 GiB per 8k conversation, so about 37 concurrent conversations in 40 GB. Without GQA (32 KV heads) each conversation needs 4 GiB and only 9 fit — GQA's 4× reduction translates directly into 4× more concurrent users, and into faster decode, because at long context the cache is read every step just like the weights.
qa: E
Why is it valid to cache keys and values during generation?

Because of the causal mask, a token's hidden states at every layer depend only on itself and earlier tokens. Generating new tokens never changes the representations of old ones, so their keys and values can be computed once and reused.
M
Prefill versus decode — which is compute-bound and which memory-bound?

Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel, so each weight read is reused across many tokens: compute-bound. Decode produces one token per sequence per step and must read every weight (and the whole KV cache) each step: memory-bandwidth-bound, which is why batching helps decode so much.
M
What goes wrong with the causal mask when you add a KV cache?

Queries and keys now have different lengths: T new queries against S = past + T keys. The mask must allow query t to see keys 0 through S − T + t. Using tril(ones(T, S)) masks the cached past instead of the future and silently corrupts outputs; positional offsets must continue from S − T as well.
H
What breaks when you batch generation of prompts with different lengths, and how is it handled?

Sequences end at different positions, so naive batching misaligns positions and lets tokens attend to padding. Simple implementations left-pad, pass an attention mask and per-sequence position ids. Serving engines instead keep ragged per-sequence caches (PagedAttention) and use continuous batching so finished sequences leave and new ones join at every step.

sum: Train merges by counting pairs, encode by applying merges in rank order, decode through the byte table.
primer:
What a tokenizer must do

Turn any string into a sequence of integers from a fixed vocabulary, and back. Words are too many (and new ones appear constantly); characters make sequences very long. Subword tokenization sits in between: frequent words become one token, rare words are split into pieces.

Byte-pair encoding, the algorithm

  1. Start from the UTF-8 bytes of the training text: 256 base tokens, so any string — any language, any emoji — can be represented and nothing is ever out of vocabulary.
  2. Count every adjacent pair of tokens. Merge the most frequent pair into a new token everywhere it occurs.
  3. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size (GPT-2: 50,257; GPT-4o: ~200k).

The output of training is an ordered list of merges. That order is the model's tokenizer.

Encoding new text

Start from bytes and repeatedly apply the earliest-learned merge that is present, until no merge applies. Applying merges in training order reproduces exactly how training segmented the text, which is what the model learned on.

Why it matters

Many LLM quirks are tokenizer artefacts: models struggle to count letters (“strawberry” is two or three tokens, not ten letters), arithmetic depends on how digits are chunked, and languages under-represented in the tokenizer's training data need several times more tokens for the same meaning — which costs more and fits less in the context window.
body:
The problem

“Implement byte-level BPE: train(text, n_merges), encode, decode.” Clarify: byte-level or character-level, tie-breaking between equally frequent pairs, and whether to pre-tokenise (split into words first). Pre-tokenise — the last test shows what happens if you do not: on repetitive text, merges run straight across word boundaries until a single token spans half a sentence.

Reference implementation

import re
from collections import Counter

# a simplified GPT-2 pre-tokeniser: words with their leading space, numbers, punctuation, whitespace
SPLIT = re.compile(r" ?[^\W\d_]+| ?\d+| ?[^\s\w]+|_+|\s+(?!\S)|\s+")

def chunks(text, pretokenize=True):
    return SPLIT.findall(text) if pretokenize else [text]

def merge(ids, pair, new_id):
    """Replace every non-overlapping occurrence of `pair`, left to right."""
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(ids):
        if i + 1 < len(ids) and ids[i] == pair[0] and ids[i + 1] == pair[1]:
            out.append(new_id); i += 2
        else:
            out.append(ids[i]); i += 1
    return out

def train_bpe(text, n_merges, pretokenize=True):
    words = Counter(chunks(text, pretokenize))              # each distinct chunk once, with its count
    seqs = {w: list(w.encode("utf-8")) for w in words}      # 256 byte tokens: nothing is ever unknown
    merges = {}                                             # (a, b) -> new id, in the order learned
    for new_id in range(256, 256 + n_merges):
        counts = Counter()
        for w, freq in words.items():                       # pairs never cross a chunk boundary
            for pair in zip(seqs[w], seqs[w][1:]):
                counts[pair] += freq
        if not counts:
            break
        pair = max(counts, key=counts.get)                  # ties: first pair counted wins
        if counts[pair] < 2:
            break                                           # a pair seen once compresses nothing
        merges[pair] = new_id
        seqs = {w: merge(ids, pair, new_id) for w, ids in seqs.items()}
    return merges, seqs

def encode_chunk(chunk, merges):
    ids = list(chunk.encode("utf-8"))
    while len(ids) >= 2:
        pair = min(zip(ids, ids[1:]), key=lambda p: merges.get(p, float("inf")))   # earliest-learned merge
        if pair not in merges:
            break
        ids = merge(ids, pair, merges[pair])
    return ids

def encode(text, merges, pretokenize=True):
    return [t for c in chunks(text, pretokenize) for t in encode_chunk(c, merges)]

def build_vocab(merges):
    vocab = {i: bytes([i]) for i in range(256)}
    for (a, b), new_id in sorted(merges.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1]):
        vocab[new_id] = vocab[a] + vocab[b]
    return vocab

def decode(ids, merges):
    vocab = build_vocab(merges)
    return b"".join(vocab[i] for i in ids).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")

Check it

# the textbook example: the first merge is the most frequent pair, 'aa'
merges, _ = train_bpe("aaabdaaabac", 3)
assert list(merges)[0] == (ord("a"), ord("a"))

text = ("the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. the dog sleeps; the fox runs. " * 20
        + "tokenization turns text into integers, and integers back into text. ")
merges, seqs = train_bpe(text, 60)

for chunk, ids in seqs.items():
    assert encode_chunk(chunk, merges) == ids                # rank-order encoding reproduces training
for s in [text, "unseen words: zebra, quixotic!", "emoji 🙂 and नमस्ते", "a_b  c\n", ""]:
    assert "".join(chunks(s)) == s                           # the pre-tokeniser never drops a character
    assert decode(encode(s, merges), merges) == s            # lossless round trip, any input
assert len(encode(text, merges)) < len(text.encode("utf-8")) / 3   # it compresses

vocab = build_vocab(merges)
assert b" the" in vocab.values()                             # a frequent word became one token
assert all(b" " not in v[1:] for k, v in vocab.items() if k >= 256)   # no token spans two words

# without pre-tokenisation, repeated text grows tokens across word boundaries
raw, _ = train_bpe(text, 60, pretokenize=False)
assert b"fox jumps over" in max(build_vocab(raw).values(), key=len)

Complexity

  • Training is O(merges × total bytes of the distinct chunks): counting each distinct word once, weighted by its frequency, is the first big saving over scanning the raw text. Production trainers also keep pair counts in a priority queue and update only the pairs next to each merge.
  • Encoding is O(n²) in the worst case per chunk, but n is a word's length, and real encoders cache the result for each distinct chunk.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Byte-level base vocabulary, and the reason: no unknown token, ever.
  • Encode by merge rank, not longest match. Greedy longest-match can produce segmentations the model never saw in training. The equivalence test (encode(text) == training ids) proves the rank-order encoder is faithful.
  • errors="replace" in decode: a model can emit a token sequence that stops in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character, especially when streaming.
  • Non-overlapping, left-to-right merging — "aaa" with the pair aa becomes [aa, a], not two overlapping pairs.
  • A lossless pre-tokeniser: every character must land in some chunk. The regex has a catch-all for each character class, and the test checks "".join(chunks(s)) == s on awkward inputs (underscores, double spaces, Devanagari combining marks).
deep:
What real tokenizers add

  • The real pre-tokeniser: GPT-2's pattern uses Unicode property classes (\p{L}, \p{N}, via the regex module) and special-cases English contractions ('s, 't, 're), so “dog.”, “dog!” and “dog?” all share the token for “dog”. GPT-4-era patterns also split numbers into chunks of at most three digits and treat newlines separately, which matters a lot for code.
  • Special tokens (<|endoftext|>, chat-role markers) are matched before BPE and never produced by merging — and must never be produced from user text, or users can forge role boundaries (a prompt-injection vector).
  • SentencePiece treats the input as a raw stream with spaces as a visible symbol (▁), and supports both BPE and the unigram language-model algorithm, which prunes a large vocabulary by likelihood instead of growing it by merges.
  • Digits: LLaMA-style tokenizers split every digit into its own token, which helps arithmetic; others chunk digits, which makes numbers shorter but misaligns place value.

Failure modes to be able to explain

  • Glitch tokens: tokens that were frequent in the tokenizer's training data but rare in the model's (the famous “SolidGoldMagikarp”) have nearly untrained embeddings and produce bizarre behaviour.
  • Trailing whitespace: ending a prompt with a space can split a token the model would normally generate as a unit (“ Paris”), degrading completions.
  • The multilingual tax: text in scripts under-represented in tokenizer training (many Indic, African and South-East Asian languages) takes several times more tokens — higher cost, shorter effective context, often worse quality. Larger vocabularies (Gemma, GPT-4o) partly fix it.

Vocabulary size is a trade-off

A larger vocabulary shortens sequences (cheaper attention, longer effective context) but enlarges the embedding and output matrices and spreads training signal over more rare tokens. The trend has been upward: 32k (LLaMA 2) → 128k (LLaMA 3) → 200k+.

Work it out

Train your tokenizer on English only, then measure bytes per token on an English sentence and on a Hindi sentence of similar meaning. What does the difference mean for cost and context length, and what would fix it?

Answer 
english = "the weather is very nice today and we are going to the market together. "
hindi = "आज मौसम बहुत अच्छा है और हम साथ में बाज़ार जा रहे हैं। "
merges_en, _ = train_bpe(english * 30, 80)

def chars_per_token(s, m):
    return len(s) / len(encode(s, m))

en_rate, hi_rate = chars_per_token(english, merges_en), chars_per_token(hindi, merges_en)
assert en_rate > 3 * hi_rate                       # English packs several characters per token
assert len(encode(hindi, merges_en)) == len(hindi.encode("utf-8"))   # Hindi falls back to raw bytes

No merge ever involved Devanagari bytes, so every Hindi character costs its full three UTF-8 bytes as three tokens, while English packs several characters into each token. The same sentence is several times more tokens in Hindi: higher API cost, less text per context window, slower generation. The fix is in the tokenizer's training mix — include the languages you serve, or use a larger multilingual vocabulary — which is why newer models with 200k-token vocabularies show big efficiency gains for Indic languages.
qa: E
Why byte-level BPE rather than character-level?

Starting from the 256 UTF-8 bytes means any string in any script, including emoji and binary junk, can be encoded with no unknown token. Character-level bases need a huge base alphabet for Unicode and still hit unseen characters.
M
Why must encoding apply merges in the order they were learned?

The model was trained on text segmented by applying merges in rank order. Applying the earliest-learned merge first reproduces that segmentation exactly; greedy longest-match or other orders can produce token sequences the model never saw, degrading quality.
M
What is pre-tokenisation and why does GPT-2 use a regex before BPE?

Splitting text into chunks (words, numbers, punctuation, whitespace) before BPE stops merges from crossing boundaries, so 'dog.' and 'dog!' share 'dog' rather than learning separate tokens, and it makes encoding cacheable per word. It also shapes how numbers and spaces are tokenised.
H
How do tokenizer choices show up as model failures?

Letter counting and spelling fail because words are opaque tokens; arithmetic suffers when digits are chunked inconsistently; glitch tokens with untrained embeddings cause bizarre outputs; trailing spaces in prompts split natural tokens; and under-represented languages need several times more tokens, raising cost and cutting effective context.

t: Decoding: temperature, top-k, top-p and beam search
sum: Turn logits into the next token four ways, then find the sequence greedy search misses.
primer:
From logits to a token

At each step the model outputs a logit for every vocabulary token. The decoding strategy decides which token to emit.

  • Greedy: always the most likely token. Deterministic, often repetitive.
  • Temperature: divide logits by T before the softmax. T < 1 sharpens the distribution (more predictable), T > 1 flattens it (more random), T → 0 is greedy.
  • Top-k: keep only the k most likely tokens, renormalise, sample.
  • Top-p (nucleus): keep the smallest set of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, renormalise, sample. The set is small when the model is confident and large when it is not — which top-k cannot do.

Beam search

Keep the B best partial sequences (by total log-probability) instead of one; extend each by every candidate token; keep the best B again. It finds higher-likelihood sequences than greedy, which is right for translation and speech recognition, where one correct output exists. For open-ended text it produces bland, repetitive output, because the most likely text is not the most human-like.

Length normalisation

Every token adds a negative log-probability, so raw scores favour short sequences. Beam search divides by a length penalty (for example ((5 + len)/6)^α from Google's NMT system) before comparing finished hypotheses.
body:
The problem

“Given next-token logits, implement greedy, temperature, top-k and top-p sampling. Then implement beam search over a model you can query for next-token log-probabilities.” Clarify: the order of the filters (temperature first, then top-k, then top-p, as in Hugging Face), and tie handling at the top-k boundary.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def sample_next(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=0, top_p=1.0, rng=None):
    logits = np.asarray(logits, float)
    if temperature == 0:
        return int(logits.argmax())                          # greedy
    z = logits / temperature
    if top_k:
        kth = np.sort(z)[-top_k]
        z = np.where(z < kth, -np.inf, z)                     # keep the k largest (ties at the edge survive)
    p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
    if top_p < 1.0:
        order = np.argsort(-p)
        cum = np.cumsum(p[order])
        keep = order[:np.searchsorted(cum, top_p) + 1]        # smallest prefix with mass >= top_p
        mask = np.zeros(len(p), bool); mask[keep] = True
        p = np.where(mask, p, 0.0); p /= p.sum()
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    return int(rng.choice(len(p), p=p))

def beam_search(next_logprobs, bos, eos, beam=3, max_len=10, alpha=0.6):
    """next_logprobs(seq) -> log-probabilities over the vocabulary for the next token."""
    live, finished = [([bos], 0.0)], []
    for _ in range(max_len):
        candidates = []
        for seq, score in live:
            lp = next_logprobs(seq)
            for tok in np.argsort(-lp)[:beam]:               # only the top `beam` extensions can survive
                candidates.append((seq + [int(tok)], score + float(lp[tok])))
        candidates.sort(key=lambda c: -c[1])
        live = []
        for seq, score in candidates:
            if seq[-1] == eos:
                finished.append((seq, score))
            elif len(live) < beam:
                live.append((seq, score))
        if not live:
            break
    finished += live                                          # unfinished beams at max_len still count
    length_penalty = lambda c: ((5 + len(c[0])) / 6) ** alpha
    return max(finished, key=lambda c: c[1] / length_penalty(c))

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
logits = np.log(np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]))

assert sample_next(logits, temperature=0) == 0
assert all(sample_next(logits, top_k=1, rng=rng) == 0 for _ in range(50))

# top-p = 0.75 keeps {0, 1} (0.5 < 0.75 <= 0.8), renormalised to 0.625 / 0.375
draws = np.array([sample_next(logits, top_p=0.75, rng=rng) for _ in range(20_000)])
assert set(np.unique(draws)) == {0, 1}
assert abs((draws == 0).mean() - 0.625) < 0.015

# temperature changes entropy in the expected direction
def entropy(T):
    p = np.exp(logits / T); p /= p.sum()
    return -(p * np.log(p)).sum()
assert entropy(0.5) < entropy(1.0) < entropy(2.0)

# a model where greedy is a trap: 'A' looks best (0.6) but every continuation after it is weak
BOS, A, B, X, Y, EOS = range(6)
table = {(BOS,): {A: 0.6, B: 0.4}, (BOS, A): {X: 0.35, Y: 0.35, EOS: 0.3}, (BOS, B): {X: 0.95, EOS: 0.05}}
def next_logprobs(seq):
    dist = table.get(tuple(seq), {EOS: 1.0})
    lp = np.full(6, -1e9)
    for tok, prob in dist.items():
        lp[tok] = np.log(prob)
    return lp

greedy = [BOS]
while greedy[-1] != EOS and len(greedy) < 5:
    greedy.append(int(next_logprobs(greedy).argmax()))
best_seq, best_score = beam_search(next_logprobs, BOS, EOS, beam=2, alpha=0.0)
assert greedy == [BOS, A, X, EOS] and np.isclose(np.exp(best_score), 0.4 * 0.95)
assert best_seq == [BOS, B, X, EOS]                           # 0.38 beats greedy's 0.6 * 0.35 = 0.21

Complexity

  • Sampling: O(V) for temperature and top-k with a partial selection; O(V log V) for top-p's sort (production kernels avoid a full sort).
  • Beam search: B model calls per step (batched in practice) and O(B²) candidates to rank; the model calls dominate.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Apply filters to logits, sample from renormalised probabilities. Masked tokens get −∞ logits, i.e. exactly zero probability.
  • Top-p always keeps at least one token — the + 1 after searchsorted — or a peaked distribution with p below the top probability would keep nothing.
  • Test sampling statistically: check the support exactly and the frequencies within a tolerance, with a fixed seed.
  • Construct a case where greedy fails to prove beam search does something. The trap model above is the standard way to show it.
deep:
Choosing a strategy

  • Closed tasks (extraction, classification, code with tests, tool calls): temperature 0 or low, and constrained decoding when output must match a schema.
  • Open-ended generation: temperature around 0.7–1.0 with top-p 0.9–0.95. Holtzman et al. showed that likelihood-maximising decoding produces degenerate, repetitive text, while nucleus sampling matches human text statistics better.
  • Min-p: keep tokens with probability at least min_p × p_max. It adapts to confidence like top-p but scales better at high temperatures; now common in open-source serving stacks.
  • Repetition and presence penalties down-weight tokens already generated; they are blunt tools — tune carefully or they damage code and structured output.

Structured and constrained decoding

To guarantee valid JSON or a grammar, compute at each step which tokens can continue a valid prefix (a finite-state machine or pushdown automaton over the token vocabulary) and mask the rest. Libraries such as Outlines and XGrammar precompile the grammar so the mask costs microseconds per step. The subtlety is token/character misalignment: a single token can span several grammar symbols.

Speculative decoding keeps the distribution exact

A small draft model proposes several tokens; the large model scores them all in one pass. Accept draft token x with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); on the first rejection, sample from the normalised residual max(0, p − q). The output distribution is provably identical to sampling from the large model alone, while several tokens are produced per large-model pass.

Beam search at scale

Beams are batched as one forward pass; KV caches are reordered (or shared via copy-on-write blocks) as beams are pruned. Diverse beam search adds a penalty for beams sharing tokens, because vanilla beams tend to be near-duplicates.

Work it out

Implement min-p sampling: keep only tokens whose probability is at least min_p times the top token's probability. Show how the kept set adapts between a confident and an uncertain distribution, compared with top-k = 3.

Answer 
def min_p_filter(logits, min_p=0.1, temperature=1.0):
    z = np.asarray(logits, float) / temperature
    p = np.exp(z - z.max()); p /= p.sum()
    keep = p >= min_p * p.max()
    p = np.where(keep, p, 0.0)
    return p / p.sum()

confident = np.log(np.array([0.90, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.01]))
uncertain = np.log(np.array([0.22, 0.21, 0.20, 0.19, 0.18]))
assert (min_p_filter(confident) > 0).sum() == 1             # only the obvious token survives
assert (min_p_filter(uncertain) > 0).sum() == 5             # every plausible option survives
# top-k = 3 keeps three either way: two junk tokens when confident, drops two good ones when unsure

Min-p's threshold is relative to the model's own confidence, so the candidate set shrinks to one when the model is sure and stays wide when it is not. Top-k keeps a fixed count regardless. Top-p also adapts, but at high temperature it admits a long tail of junk because the tail's cumulative mass grows; min-p's rule keeps rejecting tokens far below the top one, which is why it holds up better for creative high-temperature sampling.
qa: E
What does temperature do mathematically?

It divides the logits by T before the softmax. T < 1 exaggerates differences between logits, concentrating probability on the top tokens; T > 1 shrinks them, flattening the distribution; T → 0 approaches greedy argmax. The ranking of tokens never changes.
M
Why is top-p usually preferred to top-k?

Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens regardless of confidence: too many when the model is sure (admitting junk) and too few when many continuations are plausible. Top-p keeps the smallest set covering a fixed probability mass, so the candidate set adapts to the shape of the distribution.
M
Why is beam search good for translation but poor for open-ended chat?

Beam search approximates the most likely sequence. Translation and speech recognition have one correct output that high likelihood tracks well. Open-ended text's most likely continuation is generic and repetitive — likelihood-maximising decoding degenerates — so sampling with temperature and top-p produces better text.
H
How does speculative decoding keep the output distribution exactly the same as the large model's?

Each draft token x is accepted with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), where p is the target and q the draft distribution; on rejection, a replacement is sampled from the normalised residual max(0, p − q). This rejection-sampling scheme yields exactly p, and the large model verifies all draft tokens in one forward pass.

sum: A frozen weight plus a trainable rank-r product, zero-initialised, with its gradients, training loop and merge.
primer:
The problem LoRA solves

Fine-tuning every weight of a 7B model means storing gradients and optimiser state for 7 billion parameters (about 16 bytes each with Adam) and a full copy of the model for every fine-tuned variant. LoRA observes that the change needed during fine-tuning tends to have low rank, and trains only that change.

The mechanism

For a frozen weight W of shape (d_in, d_out), add a trainable update ΔW = A·B with A (d_in, r) and B (r, d_out), where the rank r is small (8–64). The layer computes y = x·W + (α/r)·(x·A)·B.

  • Trainable parameters: r·(d_in + d_out) instead of d_in·d_out. For a 4096×4096 matrix at r = 8, that is 0.39%.
  • Initialisation: A random, B zero, so ΔW = 0 and training starts exactly at the pretrained model.
  • Scaling α/r keeps the update's magnitude comparable when you change the rank, so the learning rate does not need retuning.
  • Merging: after training, W + (α/r)·A·B is an ordinary matrix — zero extra inference cost.

QLoRA in one line

Store the frozen W in 4-bit (NF4), dequantise on the fly for the forward pass, and train LoRA adapters in bf16 on top. A 65B model fine-tunes on a single 48 GB GPU.
body:
The problem

“Implement a LoRA linear layer: forward pass, gradients for the adapter only, and merging. Show it can learn a low-rank update.” Clarify the initialisation and scaling conventions, and compute (x·A)·B in that order — never materialise A·B during training.

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

class LoRALinear:
    """y = x W + (alpha / r) · (x A) B, with W frozen; A (d_in, r), B (r, d_out)."""

    def __init__(self, W, r=8, alpha=16, seed=0):
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.W = W                                           # pretrained weight, never updated
        d_in, d_out = W.shape
        self.A = rng.normal(0, 1 / np.sqrt(d_in), (d_in, r))  # random
        self.B = np.zeros((r, d_out))                        # zero: the adapter starts as a no-op
        self.scale = alpha / r
        self.merged = False

    def __call__(self, x):
        y = x @ self.W
        if not self.merged:
            y = y + self.scale * (x @ self.A) @ self.B       # (N, r) first: never build d_in × d_out
        return y

    def grads(self, x, dy):
        """Gradients of the loss for A and B given dL/dy. W gets none."""
        xa = x @ self.A                                      # (N, r)
        dB = self.scale * xa.T @ dy                          # (r, d_out)
        dA = self.scale * x.T @ (dy @ self.B.T)              # (d_in, r)
        return dA, dB

    def merge(self):
        self.W = self.W + self.scale * self.A @ self.B       # one matrix again: zero inference overhead
        self.merged = True

def trainable_fraction(d_in, d_out, r):
    return r * (d_in + d_out) / (d_in * d_out)

Check it

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d_in, d_out, N = 32, 24, 256
W = rng.normal(size=(d_in, d_out))
x = rng.normal(size=(N, d_in))

layer = LoRALinear(W, r=4, alpha=8)
assert np.allclose(layer(x), x @ W)                          # zero-initialised B: exact no-op at start

# gradient check on 0.5 * ||y - t||^2 / N, with B made non-zero first
layer.B = rng.normal(size=layer.B.shape) * 0.1
t = rng.normal(size=(N, d_out))
loss = lambda: 0.5 * ((layer(x) - t) ** 2).sum() / N
dA, dB = layer.grads(x, (layer(x) - t) / N)
for P, G in ((layer.A, dA), (layer.B, dB)):
    for i in [(0, 0), (3, 2), (P.shape[0] - 1, P.shape[1] - 1)]:
        old = P[i]; P[i] = old + 1e-6; lp = loss(); P[i] = old - 1e-6; lm = loss(); P[i] = old
        assert abs((lp - lm) / 2e-6 - G[i]) < 1e-6

# learn a genuine rank-4 update with rank-4 adapters
delta = rng.normal(size=(d_in, 4)) @ rng.normal(size=(4, d_out)) * 0.3
target = x @ (W + delta)
lora = LoRALinear(W, r=4, alpha=8, seed=1)
first = None
for step in range(3000):
    err = lora(x) - target
    cur = 0.5 * (err ** 2).sum() / N
    first = cur if first is None else first
    dA, dB = lora.grads(x, err / N)
    lora.A -= 0.01 * dA; lora.B -= 0.01 * dB
assert cur < 1e-3 * first                                   # recovers the low-rank change

before = lora(x); lora.merge()
assert np.allclose(lora(x), before)                          # merging changes nothing but speed
assert round(100 * trainable_fraction(4096, 4096, 8), 2) == 0.39

Complexity

  • Extra forward cost: O(N·r·(d_in + d_out)), small next to the base O(N·d_in·d_out).
  • Memory saving is in optimiser state and gradients: only r·(d_in + d_out) parameters need them. Activation memory is roughly unchanged — it is still needed to backpropagate through the frozen layers.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Why B = 0, A random: the model starts exactly at the pretrained weights, and B still receives gradient (because x·A ≠ 0). Both zero would leave both gradients zero forever — see the exercise.
  • Multiply (x·A)·B, not x·(A·B): the second builds a full d_in × d_out matrix every step and throws away the savings.
  • Merge for deployment, and say when you would not: when serving many adapters on one base model.
  • Test the no-op at initialisation and the merge equivalence — both are exact identities, so they make strong tests.
deep:
What LoRA learns, and what it does not

  • Updates confined to rank r cannot express high-rank changes. For style, format and task adaptation that is plenty; for teaching substantial new knowledge (continued pretraining on a new domain or language), full fine-tuning learns more. “LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less” (2024) quantifies both halves — and the second half is a feature: less catastrophic forgetting.
  • Where to put adapters: early work adapted only the attention Q and V projections; current practice targets all linear layers (attention and MLP), which closes much of the gap to full fine-tuning at small extra cost.
  • Rank and learning rate: LoRA typically wants a learning rate about 10× that of full fine-tuning. rsLoRA scales by α/√r instead of α/r so higher ranks actually help rather than being damped.

Serving many adapters

  • Merging produces one full model per adapter — fine for one customer, wasteful for thousands.
  • Multi-LoRA serving (S-LoRA, Punica, vLLM's LoRA support) keeps one base model on the GPU and applies different small adapters to different requests in the same batch, using custom kernels for the batched low-rank products. Adapters are swapped between CPU and GPU memory like pages.

The family

  • QLoRA: 4-bit NF4 base weights, double quantisation of the scaling constants, and paged optimiser states — the memory recipe for single-GPU fine-tuning.
  • DoRA: decompose each weight into magnitude and direction and apply LoRA to the direction; often closer to full fine-tuning at the same rank.
  • Prefix/prompt tuning and IA³: even fewer parameters, usually weaker.

Work it out

(a) Show in code what happens if both A and B are initialised to zero. (b) Estimate the GPU memory to QLoRA-fine-tune a 65B model: 4-bit base weights, rank-16 adapters on all linear layers (assume adapters total 0.4% of parameters), trained with Adam in fp32.

Answer 
dead = LoRALinear(W, r=4)
dead.A[:] = 0.0                                              # both factors zero
dA, dB = dead.grads(x, rng.normal(size=(N, d_out)))
assert np.all(dA == 0) and np.all(dB == 0)                   # stuck: no gradient can ever flow

params = 65e9
base_gb = params * 0.5 / 1e9                                 # 4-bit weights: 32.5 GB
adapter = 0.004 * params                                     # 260M trainable parameters
adapter_gb = adapter * (4 + 4 + 4 + 4) / 1e9                 # fp32 weights, grads, Adam m and v: ~4.2 GB
assert round(base_gb, 1) == 32.5 and round(adapter_gb, 1) == 4.2

(a) dB is proportional to x·A and dA to B; with both zero, both gradients are zero and nothing ever moves. One factor must be non-zero; making it A (with B = 0) keeps the initial function unchanged. (b) About 32.5 GB for the frozen base plus about 4 GB for the adapters and their optimiser state — roughly 37 GB before activations, which is why QLoRA fits a 65B fine-tune on a 48 GB GPU with gradient checkpointing, whereas full fine-tuning at 16 bytes per parameter would need over a terabyte.
qa: E
Why is LoRA's B matrix initialised to zero?

So that ΔW = A·B = 0 at the start and the adapted model is exactly the pretrained model; fine-tuning then begins from known-good behaviour. A is random so that B still receives a non-zero gradient — initialising both to zero would leave both gradients zero forever.
M
Why does merging make LoRA free at inference, and when would you not merge?

W + (α/r)·A·B is an ordinary weight matrix of the original shape, so the merged model has exactly the base model's cost. You keep adapters unmerged when serving many adapters on one base model — multi-LoRA serving batches requests for different adapters over shared base weights.
M
What does the α/r scaling do?

It keeps the magnitude of the update roughly constant as you change the rank, so the learning rate and α do not need retuning with r. rsLoRA argues α/√r is the right scaling for higher ranks to be useful.
H
How does LoRA fine-tuning differ from full fine-tuning in what it learns?

Updates are restricted to low rank, so LoRA adapts style, format and task behaviour well but absorbs less new knowledge in continued pretraining-style training; it also forgets less of the base model's abilities. Targeting all linear layers, higher ranks and a higher learning rate narrow the gap.

sum: An inverted-index BM25, cosine top-k, and reciprocal rank fusion — the three pieces of hybrid search.
primer:
Two ways to find relevant documents

  • Lexical (sparse): score documents by the query words they contain. BM25 is the standard. It is exact about rare terms — product codes, names, error messages — and needs no training.
  • Dense: embed query and documents as vectors with a neural model and rank by cosine similarity. It matches meaning (“car” finds “automobile”) but can miss exact identifiers.

Production RAG systems use both — hybrid retrieval — and merge the rankings.

BM25 in plain words

For each query term in a document, multiply two things:

  • IDF — how rare the term is across the collection. Matching “the” means nothing; matching “quaternion” means a lot.
  • Saturating term frequency — tf·(k1 + 1) / (tf + k1·(1 − b + b·len/avg_len)). The second occurrence of a word helps less than the first, and the tenth barely helps (k1 controls how fast it saturates). Long documents are penalised because they match more by chance (b controls how much).

An inverted index makes it fast

Map each term to the list of documents containing it (its postings). A query only touches the postings of its own terms, not every document.

Reciprocal rank fusion

BM25 scores and cosine similarities are on incomparable scales, so do not add them. RRF uses only ranks: each document scores Σ 1/(k + rank) across the lists, with k = 60. Documents that appear near the top of several lists rise.
body:
The problem

“Implement BM25 search over a small corpus, a dense top-k retriever over embeddings, and a way to combine them.” Clarify: tokenisation, the BM25 parameter values, and whether the dense side needs an ANN index (not for this size).

Reference implementation

import math
import re
from collections import Counter
import numpy as np

def tokenize(s):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", s.lower())

class BM25:
    def __init__(self, docs, k1=1.5, b=0.75):
        self.k1, self.b = k1, b
        tfs = [Counter(tokenize(d)) for d in docs]
        self.doc_len = np.array([sum(tf.values()) for tf in tfs], float)
        self.avg_len = self.doc_len.mean()
        df = Counter(term for tf in tfs for term in tf)
        N = len(docs)
        # Lucene's IDF: log(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)) — never negative
        self.idf = {t: math.log(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5)) for t, n in df.items()}
        self.postings = {}                                   # inverted index: term -> [(doc, tf)]
        for d, tf in enumerate(tfs):
            for term, count in tf.items():
                self.postings.setdefault(term, []).append((d, count))

    def search(self, query, k=5):
        scores = Counter()
        for term in set(tokenize(query)):
            for d, tf in self.postings.get(term, []):        # touch only documents containing the term
                norm = self.k1 * (1 - self.b + self.b * self.doc_len[d] / self.avg_len)
                scores[d] += self.idf[term] * tf * (self.k1 + 1) / (tf + norm)
        return scores.most_common(k)

def dense_top_k(query_vec, doc_vecs, k=5):
    q = query_vec / np.linalg.norm(query_vec)
    D = doc_vecs / np.linalg.norm(doc_vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sims = D @ q                                             # cosine similarity to every document
    k = min(k, len(sims))
    top = np.argpartition(-sims, k - 1)[:k]                  # O(n) selection, then sort only k
    top = top[np.argsort(-sims[top])]
    return [(int(i), float(sims[i])) for i in top]

def rrf(rankings, k=60):
    """Reciprocal rank fusion of several ranked lists of doc ids."""
    score = Counter()
    for ranking in rankings:
        for rank, doc in enumerate(ranking):
            score[doc] += 1.0 / (k + rank + 1)
    return [d for d, _ in score.most_common()]

Check it

docs = [
    "error E1234 occurs when the disk quota is exceeded",
    "how to reset your password and recover the account",
    "the disk is full: free space by deleting old logs",
    "password reset links expire after one hour",
    "quota exceeded error when uploading large files to storage",
]
bm = BM25(docs)
assert bm.search("E1234", 1)[0][0] == 0                     # a rare exact token wins outright
assert {d for d, _ in bm.search("password reset", 2)} == {1, 3}

# scores equal the formula computed directly for every document
def direct(q, d):
    tf, L = Counter(tokenize(docs[d])), len(tokenize(docs[d]))
    return sum(bm.idf[t] * tf[t] * (bm.k1 + 1) / (tf[t] + bm.k1 * (1 - bm.b + bm.b * L / bm.avg_len))
               for t in set(tokenize(q)) if t in tf)
for d, s in bm.search("disk quota exceeded error", 5):
    assert np.isclose(s, direct("disk quota exceeded error", d))

# term-frequency saturation: ten repetitions are worth far less than ten times one
sat = BM25(["cat", "cat " * 10, "dog", "bird", "fish"])
one, ten = sat.search("cat", 2)[1][1], sat.search("cat", 2)[0][1]
assert one < ten < 3 * one

# dense top-k agrees with a full sort
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
V, qv = rng.normal(size=(500, 32)), rng.normal(size=32)
full = np.argsort(-(V / np.linalg.norm(V, axis=1, keepdims=True)) @ (qv / np.linalg.norm(qv)))[:10]
assert [i for i, _ in dense_top_k(qv, V, 10)] == list(full)

# fusion: a document ranked well by both lists beats one ranked first by only one
assert rrf([["a", "b", "c"], ["b", "d", "a"]])[0] == "b"

Complexity

  • BM25 query: proportional to the total length of the query terms' postings lists — tiny for rare terms, large for common ones (which is why stop words are often dropped).
  • Dense exact search: O(n·d) per query; an ANN index makes it sub-linear.
  • RRF: linear in the total length of the ranked lists.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Use an inverted index and say why: scanning every document per query is what search engines exist to avoid.
  • Normalise embeddings once and use the dot product; cosine and dot product then agree.
  • Fuse ranks, not scores: BM25 is unbounded and corpus-dependent, cosine lives in [−1, 1]. Adding them lets one side dominate arbitrarily.
  • Explain the defaults: k1 ≈ 1.2–2.0 (saturation speed), b = 0.75 (length normalisation), RRF k = 60 (damps the dominance of rank 1).
deep:
Making BM25 fast at a billion documents

  • Postings are sorted by document id and compressed (delta encoding plus variable-byte or SIMD bit-packing).
  • Dynamic pruning: WAND and Block-Max WAND keep a threshold (the current k-th best score) and skip documents whose maximum possible score cannot beat it, using per-term and per-block score upper bounds. Top-k queries touch a small fraction of the postings.
  • Indexes are sharded by document; each shard returns its top-k and a coordinator merges them.

Beyond the basic hybrid

  • Learned sparse retrieval (SPLADE): a model assigns weights to vocabulary terms, including expansion terms not in the text, and the result is served from an inverted index — lexical precision with some semantic recall.
  • Late interaction (ColBERT): keep one vector per token and score with the sum of max-similarities; more accurate than a single vector, more storage.
  • Cross-encoder re-ranking: score the top 50–200 candidates with a model that reads the query and document together. Retrieval optimises recall; the re-ranker optimises precision at the top.
  • Weighted fusion: when you have labelled queries, a learned weighting or a convex combination of normalised scores can beat RRF; RRF is the strong default when you do not.

Evaluating retrieval

Recall@k on labelled queries measures whether the right passage is in the candidate set at all — for RAG it is the ceiling on answer quality. MRR and nDCG measure how high it ranks. BEIR showed that BM25 remains a hard baseline out of domain, which is the evidence behind hybrid search.
drill:
Work it out

Write recall_at_k and mrr over a small labelled query set and compare BM25 with fusion of BM25 and a second ranking. Why is recall@k the first metric to look at for a RAG system?

Answer 
def recall_at_k(ranked, relevant, k):
    return len(set(ranked[:k]) & relevant) / len(relevant)

def mean_reciprocal_rank(runs):
    return float(np.mean([next((1 / (i + 1) for i, d in enumerate(r) if d in rel), 0.0) for r, rel in runs]))

queries = {"disk full": {2, 0}, "reset password": {1, 3}, "uploading files over quota": {4}}
bm_runs = [([d for d, _ in bm.search(q, 5)], rel) for q, rel in queries.items()]
assert all(recall_at_k(r, rel, 5) == 1.0 for r, rel in bm_runs)
assert mean_reciprocal_rank(bm_runs) == 1.0

# fusing with a (deliberately poor) second ranking must not destroy a good first ranking at k = 5
fused = [(rrf([r, list(reversed(r))]), rel) for r, rel in bm_runs]
assert all(recall_at_k(r, rel, 5) == 1.0 for r, rel in fused)

Try the last query as “upload quota”: document 4 then ties with document 0, because without stemming “upload” does not match “uploading” — tokenisation and normalisation are part of retrieval quality, and a labelled query set is how you notice.

A generator can only use what retrieval puts in its context, so recall@k (with k equal to the number of passages you actually send) is an upper bound on the whole system's answer quality. If recall is low, no prompt or model change helps — fix chunking, the embedding model, hybrid search or query rewriting first. Once recall is high, precision metrics (MRR, nDCG) and the re-ranker decide how much noise surrounds the right passage.
qa: E
What do BM25's k1 and b parameters control?

k1 sets how quickly term frequency saturates: small k1 means repeated occurrences add little, large k1 approaches raw term counting. b sets how strongly scores are normalised by document length relative to the average: b = 0 ignores length, b = 1 fully normalises. Typical values are k1 ≈ 1.2–2 and b = 0.75.
M
Why does hybrid lexical plus dense retrieval beat either alone?

They fail differently. BM25 nails exact rare tokens — identifiers, names, error codes — but misses paraphrases; dense retrieval matches meaning but can blur exact identifiers and degrade out of domain. Combining them recovers documents either one would miss.
M
Why use reciprocal rank fusion instead of adding the scores?

BM25 scores are unbounded and depend on the corpus and query length, while cosine similarities sit in a narrow range, so a sum is dominated by whichever scale is larger. RRF uses only ranks, needs no calibration or tuning, and is robust; k = 60 damps the advantage of rank 1.
H
How does an inverted index keep BM25 fast at a billion documents?

Queries touch only the postings of their terms; postings are sorted by doc id and compressed; dynamic pruning (WAND, Block-Max WAND) uses per-term and per-block score upper bounds to skip documents that cannot enter the current top-k; and the index is sharded by document with a top-k merge.
