sum: Vectorised intersection-over-union, greedy NMS, the per-class trick, and soft-NMS.
primer:
The problem NMS solves

An object detector proposes many overlapping boxes around the same object, each with a confidence score. Non-maximum suppression keeps the best box for each object and removes the near-duplicates.

Intersection over union

For two boxes [x1, y1, x2, y2], IoU is the area of their overlap divided by the area of their union. 1 means identical, 0 means disjoint. The intersection is a rectangle whose corners are the maximum of the two top-left corners and the minimum of the two bottom-right corners — clipped at zero width or height when the boxes do not overlap.

Greedy NMS

  1. Sort boxes by score, highest first.
  2. Keep the top box. Remove every remaining box whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold (typically 0.5).
  3. Repeat with what remains.

Two refinements

  • Per-class NMS: a person and a bicycle can overlap heavily; boxes should only suppress boxes of the same class.
  • Soft-NMS: instead of deleting overlapping boxes, decay their scores by how much they overlap. In crowded scenes, where two real objects overlap, hard NMS deletes one of them.

IoU is also the standard detection metric (a prediction is correct if IoU with a ground-truth box ≥ 0.5) and the basis of box-regression losses (GIoU, DIoU).
body:
The problem

“Implement IoU between one box and many, and NMS. Then make it class-aware.” Clarify the box format ([x1, y1, x2, y2] corners versus centre/width/height) and whether coordinates are inclusive pixels (some old code adds 1 to widths).

Reference implementation

import numpy as np

def area(b):
    return (b[..., 2] - b[..., 0]) * (b[..., 3] - b[..., 1])

def iou(box, boxes):
    """box (4,), boxes (N, 4) as [x1, y1, x2, y2] -> (N,) IoU."""
    x1 = np.maximum(box[0], boxes[:, 0]); y1 = np.maximum(box[1], boxes[:, 1])
    x2 = np.minimum(box[2], boxes[:, 2]); y2 = np.minimum(box[3], boxes[:, 3])
    inter = np.clip(x2 - x1, 0, None) * np.clip(y2 - y1, 0, None)    # zero when they do not overlap
    return inter / (area(box) + area(boxes) - inter + 1e-12)

def nms(boxes, scores, iou_thresh=0.5, score_thresh=0.0):
    boxes, scores = np.asarray(boxes, float), np.asarray(scores, float)
    order = np.argsort(-scores, kind="stable")
    order = order[scores[order] >= score_thresh]
    keep = []
    while order.size:
        best, rest = order[0], order[1:]
        keep.append(int(best))
        order = rest[iou(boxes[best], boxes[rest]) <= iou_thresh]    # drop what overlaps the winner
    return keep

def batched_nms(boxes, scores, classes, iou_thresh=0.5):
    """Class-aware NMS in one call: shift each class into its own region of the plane."""
    boxes = np.asarray(boxes, float)
    offset = np.asarray(classes)[:, None] * (boxes.max() + 1)
    return nms(boxes + offset, scores, iou_thresh)

Check it

a = np.array([0, 0, 10, 10.0])
cases = np.array([[0, 0, 10, 10], [5, 0, 15, 10], [20, 20, 30, 30], [0, 0, 5, 5], [10, 0, 20, 10]], float)
assert np.allclose(iou(a, cases), [1.0, 50 / 150, 0.0, 25 / 100, 0.0])   # identical, half, disjoint, inside, touching

boxes = np.array([[0, 0, 10, 10], [1, 1, 11, 11], [0, 1, 10, 11],      # one object, three detections
                  [50, 50, 60, 60], [51, 50, 61, 60]], float)           # a second object, two detections
scores = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.85, 0.7, 0.95])
assert sorted(nms(boxes, scores)) == [0, 4]

# against a brute-force definition: kept boxes never overlap each other above the threshold,
# and every removed box overlaps some higher-scoring kept box
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
xy = rng.uniform(0, 50, (200, 2)); wh = rng.uniform(5, 20, (200, 2))
B, S = np.c_[xy, xy + wh], rng.random(200)
kept = nms(B, S, 0.4)
for i in kept:
    others = [j for j in kept if j != i]
    assert np.all(iou(B[i], B[others]) <= 0.4)
for j in set(range(200)) - set(kept):
    assert any(S[i] >= S[j] and iou(B[i], B[j:j + 1])[0] > 0.4 for i in kept)

# class-aware: a person and a bicycle in the same place both survive
cls = np.array([0, 1])
two = np.array([[0, 0, 10, 10], [1, 1, 11, 11]], float)
assert nms(two, np.array([0.9, 0.8])) == [0]
assert sorted(batched_nms(two, np.array([0.9, 0.8]), cls)) == [0, 1]

Complexity

Sorting is O(N log N); the suppression loop is O(N·K) for K kept boxes, O(N²) in the worst case. Detectors usually keep only the top few thousand boxes by score before NMS to bound it.

Details that separate a good answer

  • Clip the intersection at zero in both dimensions — otherwise two disjoint boxes can produce a positive “intersection” from two negative lengths.
  • Vectorise IoU against all remaining boxes, so the loop runs once per kept box, not per pair.
  • The offset trick for per-class NMS: shifting each class far away makes cross-class IoU exactly zero, so one NMS call does all classes (it is how torchvision's batched_nms works).
  • Test the invariant, not just one example: kept boxes are mutually below the threshold, and every suppressed box was suppressed by a higher-scoring kept one.
deep:
NMS in real detectors

  • On GPU: compute the full IoU matrix of the top-N boxes in parallel, store a suppression bitmask per box, then do the (cheap) sequential scan over bitmasks. torchvision, TensorRT and ONNX all ship an optimised NMS op.
  • Thresholds are a trade-off: a low IoU threshold suppresses real neighbouring objects in crowds (lower recall); a high one leaves duplicates (lower precision).
  • Soft-NMS decays scores (s ← s·e^(−IoU²/σ)) instead of deleting, recovering crowded objects at little cost; weighted NMS averages the coordinates of the suppressed cluster for better localisation.

Getting rid of NMS

  • DETR predicts a fixed set of boxes and trains with Hungarian matching, a one-to-one assignment between predictions and ground truth, so duplicates are penalised during training and no NMS is needed.
  • YOLOv10 trains with both one-to-many and one-to-one heads and uses only the one-to-one head at inference: NMS-free real-time detection, removing a latency and deployment headache.

IoU as a loss

Plain IoU has zero gradient when boxes do not overlap. GIoU adds a penalty based on the smallest enclosing box; DIoU and CIoU add centre-distance and aspect-ratio terms. These are standard box-regression losses in modern detectors.

Where this meets multimodal models

Open-vocabulary detectors (OWL-ViT, Grounding DINO) and vision-language models that output boxes still post-process with IoU-based suppression, and grounding benchmarks score answers by IoU with the reference box.
drill:
Work it out

Implement Gaussian soft-NMS: after picking the best box, multiply every remaining score by exp(−IoU²/σ) instead of deleting, and drop boxes only when their score falls below a small threshold. Show a crowded case where hard NMS loses a real object and soft-NMS keeps it.

Answer 
def soft_nms(boxes, scores, sigma=0.5, score_thresh=0.05):
    boxes, scores = np.asarray(boxes, float), np.asarray(scores, float).copy()
    idx, keep = np.arange(len(scores)), []
    while idx.size:
        best = idx[np.argmax(scores[idx])]
        keep.append(int(best))
        idx = idx[idx != best]
        if idx.size:
            scores[idx] *= np.exp(-iou(boxes[best], boxes[idx]) ** 2 / sigma)   # decay, do not delete
            idx = idx[scores[idx] >= score_thresh]
    return keep, scores

# two genuinely different people standing close together (IoU ~ 0.54) plus one duplicate detection
crowd = np.array([[0, 0, 10, 20], [3, 0, 13, 20], [0, 0, 10, 19.5]], float)
conf = np.array([0.95, 0.90, 0.60])
assert nms(crowd, conf, 0.5) == [0]                          # hard NMS deletes the second person
kept, decayed = soft_nms(crowd, conf)
assert kept[:2] == [0, 1] and decayed[1] > 0.45             # soft-NMS keeps them, ranked second

The second person overlaps the first with IoU ≈ 0.54, just above the hard threshold, so hard NMS deletes a real detection. Soft-NMS decays its score from 0.90 to about 0.5 — still a confident detection — while the duplicate (IoU ≈ 0.97) is decayed much more. It improves recall in crowded scenes, and average precision with it, at essentially no extra cost.
qa: E
Why do object detectors need non-maximum suppression?

Dense detectors score many anchors or grid positions, and several of them fire on the same object with slightly different boxes. NMS keeps the highest-scoring box per object and removes the overlapping duplicates, turning thousands of candidates into one detection per object.
M
What is the complexity of NMS, and how is it run on a GPU?

O(N log N) to sort and O(N·K) (worst case O(N²)) to suppress. GPU implementations compute the full IoU matrix of the top-N boxes in parallel, encode suppression as bitmasks, and do a short sequential pass over the masks; pre-filtering to the top few thousand boxes bounds N.
M
What does soft-NMS change, and when does it help?

Instead of deleting boxes that overlap the chosen one, it decays their scores as a function of IoU (linear or Gaussian). In crowded scenes where real objects overlap above the threshold, hard NMS deletes true positives; soft-NMS keeps them with reduced scores, improving recall and AP.
H
How does DETR avoid NMS?

It predicts a fixed-size set of boxes and trains with a bipartite (Hungarian) matching loss that assigns each ground-truth object to exactly one prediction; unmatched predictions are trained to predict 'no object'. Duplicates are penalised during training, so the output needs no suppression. YOLOv10 achieves NMS-free inference with a one-to-one assignment head.
